The Tribunal’s powers and discretion under the Scheme and the Sanctions Guidance to
award costs

141. Paragraph 9(8)(ii) of the Scheme confers discretionary power on the Tribunal to order
payment of ‘the whole or part of the costs of, and incidental to, the investigation and
the hearing of the Formal Complaint’ and that the Tribunal itself determines ‘the
amount to be paid’ by the Member or Member Firm. Paragraph 75 of the Sanctions
Guidance echoes the discretion conferred in the Scheme, namely, after determining
sanction, ‘a Tribunal considers whether to make an award in respect of the costs
incurred by the FRC’) (emphasis added). Paragraph 75(a) further provides inter alia

Consideration of the award of costs
ii) The approach to costs generally and to the costs claimed by Executive Counsel
144. As is apparent from the foregoing, Executive Counsel has had comprehensive success.
The Tribunal has made Adverse Findings against the Respondent on both grounds
advanced in the Formal Complaint. Accordingly, this is not a case where there was
divided success as between Executive Counsel and the Respondent. The starting point,
therefore, and in common with the usual practise that costs follow success, is that the
Respondent should bear the costs of the proceedings and investigation (ie Executive
Counsel’s Costs, as claimed). Nor was this a case involving multiple respondents
against whom different allegations were advanced or who had varying degrees of
responsibility for, or involvement in, the matters being explored before the Tribunal -
such as to justify apportioning costs among respondents. No question of allocation of
costs therefore arises in this case.

145. In relation to the question of reasonableness, which the majority of the Tribunal
considers relates to the conduct of the proceedings (and not to a respondent’s
resources), the majority begins by observing that the hearing was conducted
responsibly and with commendable efficiency. While the hearing was initially
scheduled for two days, the emergence of the several preliminary matters (prompted by
the Respondent’s communications of 6 and 12 May and his non-attendance) and the
provision for a later start on the second day to enable the Respondent to attend,
necessitated a third day (to consider sanctions). The Hearing Bundle and bundle of
authorities were well-ordered, compiled with care and had no extraneous or omitted
materials. There were no costs wasted or unnecessarily incurred. We note the
responsibility and restraint on the part of Executive Counsel in confining her costs to
those arising from the non-cooperation allegations and in declining to claim for the
costs of the investigations of the underlying matters. In the Tribunal’s view there is no
basis to support any additional abatement of the costs claimed.

it was a proportionate use of resources for Executive Counsel to bring these

paragraph 14 obligations, and which has had the benefit of clarifying that point of

Note of Reasons of Mr Duggal

153. The Tribunal was unanimous on the findings of fact which support findings on the
paragraph 14 breaches and the sanction. However, noting the EC’s (corrected)
submissions on references to Misconduct on the substantive issue, and the fact that the
Sanctions Guidance at times does not delineate Misconduct from other breaches, I find
requires a different approach on certain issues to that taken by the majority. In
particular because of the substantial discretion afforded to the Tribunal in terms of
factors it can take into account at various stages.

The EC’s submissions on breaches and Misconduct

154. Following clarification from Executive Counsel (EC) that the issue to be decided
should be restricted to a breach of paragraphs 14 (1) and (2) of the Scheme, the
Tribunal made findings of fact on the Allegations in the Formal Complaint and found
them proved, and so made Adverse Findings. However, the EC also confirmed that
references to Misconduct in its skeleton argument should be read as references to the
generic term of ‘misconduct’ (with a lower case ‘m’), rather than the defined term in
the Scheme. Also, and crucially, EC went on to write:

“For the avoidance of doubt, although Executive Counsel does not seek an Adverse
Finding on the basis of Misconduct, she contends that the acts and omissions alleged
against the Respondent fell significantly short of the standard reasonably to be expected
of the Respondent as a Member, and have brought or are likely to bring discredit to him
or to the accountancy profession, as set out in the definition of Misconduct in paragraph
2(1) of the Scheme.”

78
I accept the EC’s contention above that non-cooperation by the Respondent, an
omission, is to be assessed using the Misconduct definition in paragraph 2(1) of the
Scheme. This does not suggest to me a risk (or actual) conflation of paragraph 14 (1)
breaches with Misconduct but is a submission, which I accept, that the sanctionable
consequences of the former can be viewed through the lens of the latter (i.e.,
Misconduct, as defined).

The duty to co-operate with the Tribunal under paragraph 14 (1)

155. Paragraph 14 (1) of the Scheme says:
“Every Member …shall at all times co-operate fully with the Executive Counsel and
with any Tribunal appointed pursuant to this Scheme.” [emphasis added]

I read this to mean that a Member shall co-operate both with the EC and, separately,
with this Disciplinary Tribunal. My view is reinforced by the fact that The EC and
Disciplinary Tribunal (which is independent of the FRC) are distinct entities, the former
having delivered the Formal Complaint to the Conduct Committee and the latter
constituted by a Convener under paragraph 9 of the Scheme, to deliver its findings to the
Conduct Committee pursuant to that. It follows that a Member’s failure to co-operate
fully with this Disciplinary Tribunal is a separate breach of a separate duty owed to the
Tribunal from that owed to the EC for failing to respond to communications and comply
with a notice (essentially, for non-attendance for interview) during an investigation.

Therefore, if found, as was the case here, it must be taken into account when deciding on
sanction. Also, it should not, strictly, be treated as a factor in deciding the seriousness of
the Allegations which pertain only to the duty owed by the Respondent to the EC (the
first part of 14 (1)) during the investigation. This is reinforced by the fact that when the
Respondent committed breaches which resulted in the Formal Complaint, and so the
Allegations, he could not have owed a duty to a Tribunal because no Tribunal had been
appointed. The two are separate breaches and not one continuing breach avoiding the
problem of duplicity. Therefore, it is open to the Tribunal to sanction separately for the
second breach or, alternatively, to find that it should attract no separate sanction on some
higher principle such as, say, totality or fairness.

79
Non-cooperation with the Disciplinary Tribunal

156. The Convener, on behalf of the Tribunal, continually made attempts to communicate
with the Respondent as to the need for his attendance so that the hearing could be
effective. Also, to the requests for reasons when he prevaricated or did not respond. In
my view, the Respondent was mostly silent but also evasive in the limited messages he
sent back.

157. Examples of the Respondent’s non-cooperation with the Tribunal include omitting to a)
confirm whether or not he would attend so that the hearing could be more effective; b)
to provide credible reasons, supported by evidence, for absence on the first two days of
the hearing and the resumed hearing on sanctions (I note that there is no ultimate
obligation on the Respondent to attend), and; c) confirm receipt of communications sent
by the Tribunal via the Convener. The Respondent could have avoided these non-
cooperation failures but instead chose not to and so failed in varying degrees on all
three obligations. For these reasons, I am of the opinion that the Respondent did not
fully cooperate with the Tribunal and so failed in his duty to cooperate with it.

158. These failures postdate the conduct in the Formal Complaint and were not therefore
pleaded in the Hearing Bundle. Equally, they are not matters on which the EC could
have done much more than draw to the attention of the Tribunal at the hearing(s) due to
the fact that this form of non-cooperation occurred so late in the day. However, the
Tribunal has the discretionary power to take this into account from paragraph 9(4) of
the Scheme:

The Disciplinary Tribunal may amend the Formal Complaint either before or during
the hearing subject to the requirements of a fair hearing and in the interests of justice.

Exercising the Tribunal’s discretion on including this conduct within the Formal
Complaint, while noting the ‘requirements’, I would place non-cooperation with a
properly assembled Tribunal as pointing to the need for a material uplift on any sanction
absent such non-cooperation. Non-cooperation with the Tribunal should also be taken
into account on the question of the award of costs.

80

Intent

159. I am of the view that when deciding the appropriate sanction, it is only after a finding
of fact on the evidence that the Adverse Findings are made out, that the issue of
culpability is relevant (as are aggravating and mitigating factors). In my opinion, no
other sequence is logical because culpability can only be considered once the act or
omission has been proved through evidence. Paragraph 14 (1) simply places an
obligation that the Member “shall at all times co-operate fully” and does not address
degrees of culpability for a failure to not do so, this being dealt with - correctly in my
view - in the Sanctions Guidance. Where the Tribunal finds in its decision on merits, as
this Tribunal did, that the non-cooperation by the Respondent was ‘deliberate’, it is a
finding on culpability and not on whether the act, omission or conduct occurred. Such a
finding is highly relevant in the decision on sanction.

160. ‘Deliberate’ – a finding of this Tribunal when looking at the behaviour of the
Respondent - was to my mind used as an umbrella term. The Sanctions Guidance is
very helpful in that it distinguishes between two types of ‘deliberateness’: Intent and
Recklessness. The question to be answered is: Were the Respondent’s breaches of the
paragraph 14 obligations (and the duty owed to the Tribunal) simply recklessness on his
part or carried out with intent? The Guidance provides assistance in paragraphs 58 and
59.

161. Paragraphs 58 and 59 identify factors which tend to show whether the Misconduct (58)
or unspecified conduct (59) was either intentional or reckless. Key extracts relate to
whether the Member:
- ‘intended or foresaw that the likely…consequences of their actions or inactions would
amount to a falling short of professional standards of conduct (paragraph 58(a).
- ’permitted the Misconduct to continue notwithstanding that they knew that their actions
breached the relevant rules’ (paragraph 58(b).
- ‘repeated the Misconduct notwithstanding being aware that to do so would involve
breaching the relevant rules, standards or procedures’ (paragraph 58(f)).

81
- (a) knew that a proposed course of action or inaction might involve a breach of the
applicable professional standards, and (b) proceeded nevertheless.

This guidance identifies intent and recklessness as different degrees of culpability on the
Respondent’s part which, in my view, must be assessed in the alternative with full intent
attracting a higher sanction than mere recklessness.

That factors under the heading of intent are cited in the context of Misconduct does not
preclude them from being applied to other breaches such as those in issue here because
they are factors identified for illustrative purposes and, as such, not confined in their use.
I find them both helpful and relevant to the issue of sanction for the (two separate)
breaches identified here.

162. I find that the evidence supporting the factual determination of the non-cooperation in
the formal Complaint (which addressed only non-cooperation with the EC and resulted
in the Allegations) clearly shows that all three limbs of paragraph 58 (Intent) identified
above were present. The fact that there are references to Misconduct in paragraph 58
does not, in my view, eliminate the Tribunal’s discretion to reach a decision on
culpability for an Adverse Finding as intentional as to cooperation with the EC or the
Tribunal. The Respondent was told what co-operation entailed, was reminded of the
consequences, and despite this decided not to cooperate, in different ways, at different
times and with different entities. He knew that the consequences of his non-cooperation
would amount to a falling short of professional standards as determined by the Scheme
of which he is a Member. As regards the investigation, he continued to do so for a
significantly long period of time notwithstanding being told that his failure to engage
would amount to a breach. As such, I find that his level of culpability is “Intent” (as
defined in the Guidance) on non-cooperation both with the EC and the Tribunal. This
finding eliminates the need to assess paragraph 59, the lower level of culpability.

Initial assessment of potential sanctions

163. The next point of difference between my approach and that of the majority is the
applicability and weight to be given to the various factors identified in the initial

82
assessment of potential sanctions. They are listed in para 21 of the Guidance section
entitled: “Undertaking the initial assessment of the potential sanctions to impose”.

“In assessing the nature and seriousness of the Misconduct and in determining which
sanctions might be appropriate, a Tribunal will normally consider the factors
summarised in the next paragraph. This list is not exhaustive and not all factors will be
applicable in a particular case. A Tribunal should also consider carefully whether there
may be other factors, not listed, that are relevant. Having identified the factors that it
regards as relevant, a Tribunal should decide the relative weight to ascribe to each
relevant factor.”

164. Having heard, by way of a submission from the EC, that references to Misconduct in
the Guidance may be used when deciding on the sanction on Adverse Findings, I accept
the EC’s contention that where the Respondent is found to have committed acts and
omissions which ‘fall significantly short of the requisite standard, and have brought or
are likely to bring discredit to him or to the accountancy profession’, the para 21
factors may be considered. Whereas the majority of the Tribunal agreed that d, q and r
were potentially relevant when looking at non-cooperation with the EC, but decided not
to take them into account for reasons mentioned in their reasoning, I take a different
view. Findings of fact on paragraph 14 breaches do not, in my view, mean that these
factors have been implicitly sanctioned. I consider that not only do d, q and r apply to
the Allegations but also to the breach of non-cooperation duty to the Tribunal, and so
must be taken into account when making the initial assessment. I also find that b, d, e, j
and k. should be considered for both breaches. This because they provide colour and
texture on deciding the starting point of sanction prior to reviewing aggravating and
mitigating factors suggested in the Guidance, and the principles we extract from
relevant cases and other guidance.

As to b – “gravity and the duration of the Misconduct”, the Respondent’s breach
prevented the Investigation from being completed, an outcome which I consider to be
grave. The non-cooperation was over a number of years in duration and not restricted to
one or a few instances.

83
As to d – “involved a failure to comply with professional standards, whether such failure
was intentional or unintentional”, I am sure that the Respondent’s conduct did not meet
the minimum professional standard, and this failure was intentional.

As to e, - “the nature, extent and importance of the standards breached”, I find that
cooperation with the regulator’s reasonable request to cooperate is essential to the
effectiveness of the Scheme and a failure to do so will bring discredit to a Member and /
or the accountancy profession.

As to j - “isolated, or repeated or ongoing”, I find the Respondent’s conduct was
repeated and ongoing based on the evidence as to his failure to attend a meeting.

As to k – “the length of time”, as b and j, above both refer to ‘duration’ and ‘ongoing’,
and it is already noted that the length of time of the Respondent’s non-cooperation was a
number of years, I would not attach weight to this to avoid duplication.

Adjustment for deterrence

165. While agreeing with the sanction (in totality) proposed by colleagues, I arrive at the
conclusion on ‘Adjustment for deterrence’ via a different route. Firstly, any adjustment
should only be applied if, as the Guidance says: “the sanction arrived at, after making
any adjustment to reflect any aggravating and mitigating factors, is insufficient”.
Secondly, I am of the opinion that, as per paragraphs 66 and 67 of the Guidance,
deterrence must here be viewed as applicable in two distinct ways: deterring the
Respondent, qua Member, and, separately, the potential for deterring other Members
and Member Firms through influencing their behaviour (see 67. c). This is also
supported by the language used throughout the Guidance which distinguishes Member
from other Members and Member Firms.

Sanction

166. In my opinion, the sanction should reflect the totality of Paragraph 14 breaches in the
Allegations but also the breach of the duty owed to the Tribunal. It should of course be

84
proportionate, take account of regulatory objectives and, where suitable, the Guidance.
Starting, say, with a sanction of three years exclusion and increasing that to reflect
seriousness and aggravating factors would in practice have little, if any, deterrence
effect on the Respondent in the future for a variety of reasons. However, an uplift,
which I think is appropriate here, would send a strong signal to other Members and
Member Firms as to the seriousness of the conduct found and it is only on that basis
that it can be justified. This is consistent with the guidance in 67 c. and 67 d, the latter
aiming for ‘credible deterrence’ as applicable also to other Members and Member
Firms. For all these reasons, I agree with colleagues on the level of sanction they
propose but arrive at my decision differently.

Costs

The Scheme and Sanctions Guidance

167. Paragraph 9(8)(ii) of the Scheme does not mandate and only invites consideration as to
whether the Tribunal should make an award of costs. It also confers a wide discretion to
award the whole or part of the costs arising from, and incidental to, two sets of
activities: a) the investigation of the Formal Complaint, and b) the hearing of that
Formal Complaint, if an Adverse Finding is made (as is the case here).

168. Paragraph 75 of the Sanctions Guidance, on the other hand, refers only to a) “costs
incurred by the FRC” and b) that the Tribunal may “take account of the Member’s
financial position”. I interpret this to mean that, in order to be awarded, some evidence
that the costs were incurred by the FRC must be provided. Secondly, that the Tribunal
has the discretion as to whether to take account of the Member’s financial position. I
also note that this is guidance for the Tribunal and not a rule which must be strictly
followed.

169. There is no reference in the Scheme or Sanctions Guidance to other factors or
adjustments to be taken into account such as fairness or ensuring costs are reasonable
and proportionate to the case, which in commercial litigation provide a mechanism for
judicial control over legal costs.

85
The EC’s submissions

170. On 23 July 2025 the Tribunal received by email a document from the FRC’s Legal
services Team entitled ‘Schedule of Costs as at 18 July 2025’ for a total of £19,054.
These costs relate to Counsel (£16,298), FRC legal Assistant (£2,396) and
Disbursements (£360). There are two relevant points made in the Notes:

(i) An additional figure will be provided at the hearing for fees incurred after 18
July 2025, in preparing for and appearing at the resumed Tribunal hearing, and
(ii) this figure includes time spent on tasks partly or completely associated with the
investigation of the underlying allegations of Misconduct, rather than the failure
to co-operate. Arriving at a precise division between the two is not possible, due
to the way in which the time has been recorded.

The schedule and notes are significant for three reasons; firstly, because the Schedule
is acceptable evidence for me that the £19,054 was a cost incurred by the FRC up to
that date for investigating and hearing only the Formal Complaint; secondly, it makes
clear that Counsel’s fees for the resumed hearing were not included but would be
provided later, inferring that it anticipated incurring them for the resumed hearing and
would provide evidence, and; thirdly, that an attempt at adjustment had been made
(using estimation) to reduce the recorded costs which, it is implied, would otherwise
overstate the correct allocation for ‘time spent’ costs on investigating the Formal
Complaint and the Disciplinary Hearing arising from it.

171. Then on 23 July 2025, the Tribunal received by email a second document from the
FRC’s Legal services Team entitled ‘Tribunal Schedule of Costs as at 24 July 2025’
for a total of £37,459.79. The detailed breakdown confirms that all of these relate to the
Disciplinary Hearing, specifically Venue, Transcription, Convener, Tribunal attendance
and preparation and Expenses. The Notes state “+ TBC” against two items related to
Tribunal Members fees and expenses, presumably for items which had not been
incurred or claimed.

172. At the sanctions hearing on 24 July 2025, Mr Potts told the Tribunal, calculating on the
spot as he did so, that his fees for preparation for the resumed hearing required 3 hours

86
plus one day and that this would be £2,688 (including VAT). Various employees from
the FRC were present at the hearing but neither challenged nor explicitly confirmed that
the FRC deemed this to be incurred by it. Since then the FRC has confirmed by email
that these costs have been incurred.

The Respondent’s financial position

173. Paragraph 75 of the Sanctions Guidance allows the Tribunal discretion as to taking into
account the Respondent’s financial position when making an award of costs. Given that
the Tribunal is not bound to take this into account but may do so, the first decision
which must be made is whether the Tribunal wishes to exercise its discretion and take
into account at his financial position. No guidance is offered on how this is to be carried
out in terms of a list of factors to consider, or high-level regulatory principles, such as
is the case for sanction.

174. However, I considered the following factors in deciding the issue on the basis that
general principles of fairness and proportionality require me to do so:

1) In my view the Respondent chose not to attend the hearings. By doing so
he knowingly gave up the opportunity to put forward his case on costs,
including his financial position.
2) In the Hearing Bundle there is mention of the Respondent’s length of
employment in what was a senior financial position in a mid-size
international firm ([Company X]) for many years and that he also was
earning after leaving that firm. Moreover, we also learned that he was in
his mid-fifties in age. Even if the Tribunal has the discretion to draw
conclusions as to means from that, I would not. Neither of these are in any
practical way useful in establishing the Respondent’s financial position as
of today.
3) In an email on affordability and means on legal representation (not strictly
relevant on costs), the EC in an email made the point that to go beyond
mere assertion on means would require the Respondent to make a full
statement as to his income, assets and liabilities, and produce copies of all
documents necessary to substantiate the statement. The statement should

87
also provide details of any disposal of assets with a value in excess of
£250,000. The Tribunal could, using its discretion, have waived that high
evidential standard had the Respondent appeared before us, but he chose
not to attend the hearings and so forfeited the opportunity.

Taking account these factors that I would decline to exercise discretion to look at the
Respondent’s financial position.

Other Factors
175. I note that in civil actions in England & Wales, it is usual that costs follow the event –
the loser pays reasonable costs of his opponent. This is a ‘civil’ hearing resulting from a
contractual arrangement between Member and, ultimately, the FRC, and so my starting
position is that the Member should pay costs, subject to the Scheme rules and
Guidance. Also, that Regulatory objectives include deterring future misconduct by
ensuring that Members who commit breaches bear the financial burden of their actions.
The risk of having to pay regulatory costs from non-cooperation may encourage firms
or individuals to cooperate early and settle matters, reducing the need for lengthy
enforcement. I also note that other regulatory bodies such as the FCA and SRA can
recover costs in disciplinary cases where the respondent is found to be at fault, as is the
case here.

Award of Costs

176. Applying the relevant paragraphs of the Scheme and Sanctions Guidance, I find that the
costs in the two Schedules, £37,459.79 and £19,054, which makes a total of
£56,513.79, should be awarded in full as they are costs only in respect of the hearing of
the Formal Complaint and incurred by the FRC. They are payable to the FRC by the
Respondent within 28 days from the date of this award.

177. As to the additional amount calculated by Mr Potts in respect of his fees for the
resumed hearing on sanction of £2,688, I would add this sum given that formal
confirmation has now been received that this amount has been incurred by the FRC.

88
178. I would allow the costs referred to as “+ TBC” to be confirmed as ‘eligible for
consideration’ in a second costs award which can be done on the papers.

title: FRC imposes sanctions against BDO LLP and two audit engagement partners
text:
1
Edited for publication
IN THE MATTER OF

THE EXECUTIVE COUNSEL TO THE FINANCIAL REPORTING COUNCIL

- and -

BDO LLP

SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT

1. This Settlement Agreement (“Agreement”) is made on 8 August 2025 between
Jamie Symington as Deputy Executive Counsel of the Financial Reporting Council
(“FRC”), of 13th Floor, Exchange Tower, 1 Harbour Exchange Square, London,
E14 9GE (“the Executive Counsel”), and BDO LLP (“BDO”) (together “the
Parties”). The Agreement is evidenced by the signatures of the Parties.
2. Terms used in this Agreement shall have the same meaning as set out in the FRC
Accountancy Scheme (“the Scheme”) and the FRC Sanctions Guidance dated
March 2021 (“the 2021 Sanctions Guidance”).
3. A Formal Complaint alleging Misconduct against BDO as a member firm of the
Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (“the ICAEW”) was
delivered to the Conduct Committee under paragraph 7(11) of the Scheme on 17
April 2025. The amended Formal Complaint as submitted to the Disciplinary
Tribunal (“the Tribunal”) is annexed to this Agreement.
4. The Parties recognise that the determination to be made in this case is a matter
for the Tribunal in accordance with paragraph 8(5) of the Scheme.
5. If the decision of the Tribunal is to approve the Agreement, including the sanctions
set out below, and the proposed amendments to the Formal Complaint further to
regulation 24 of the Accountancy Regulations, then the Agreement shall take effect

2
from the next working day after the date on which the notice of the decision is sent
to the Parties in accordance with paragraph 8(5) of the Scheme.

6. The Agreement and annex shall be published in accordance with paragraph 8(6)
of the Scheme.

7. The Formal Complaint is in respect of BDO’s (i) inadequate response to evidence
that its former senior manager, Ms Amanda Nightingale (née Cleaver) (“Ms
Nightingale”) had inserted an electronic signature into an Auditor’s Report and
provided it to a client without authorisation, and to subsequent reports which raised
concerns about her integrity (ii) failures in respect of certain of its systems,
controls, policies and procedures (iii) liability for the admitted Misconduct of its
former partners, Mr John Everingham, and Mr Kevin Cook, and for the admitted
Misconduct of Ms Nightingale.
8. BDO admits the Formal Complaint and the Allegations contained within it.
Sanction
9. The Parties have agreed the following terms of settlement:

a.
a financial sanction of £6,500,000 reduced by 10% in accordance with
paragraph 73 of the 2021 Sanctions Guidance for settlement at Stage 3 to
£5,850,000, to be paid no later than 28 days after the date when this
Agreement takes effect;

b.
in relation to the audits where unauthorised audit opinions were issued by the
firm, BDO has repaid audit fees for 6 audits and will take all reasonable steps
to repay fees, where charged, in relation to the remaining audits within a
period of 56 days, and report to the FRC on those steps following the expiry
of that period;

c.
a Severe Reprimand; and

d.
the Non-Financial Sanctions set out in the Schedule to this Agreement.

10. In determining the appropriate sanctions against BDO, the Executive Counsel
adopted the approach set out in paragraph 18 of the 2021 Sanctions Guidance,
as follows:
Nature and Seriousness of the Misconduct
11. The Executive Counsel considers that the following factors are relevant to
assessing the nature and seriousness of the Misconduct:

3
a. BDO derived a financial benefit from the Misconduct insofar as they received
audit fees in respect of audits where (i) the Auditor’s Report was not signed by
the Responsible Individual (ii) inadequate audit evidence had been obtained
and/or reviewed (iii) and/or inadequate oversight and supervision was
exercised by the relevant Responsible Individual.

b. The Misconduct in aggregate in this case was extremely serious and continued
over a period of years.
c. The Misconduct at least risked the loss of significant sums of money, and
potentially adversely affected a significant number of people in the UK.
d. In the case of Ms Nightingale, the Misconduct was intentional and dishonest
and demonstrated a lack of integrity.
e. Ms Nightingale’s Misconduct, as well as that of Mr Everingham and Mr Cook,
was able to occur and remain undetected because of the circumstances
created by failings in BDO’s systems, controls, policies and procedures.
f. The Misconduct involved a failure to comply with important professional
standards. The standards breached, including the Fundamental Principles of
Integrity (by Ms Nightingale), Professional Behaviour and Professional
Competence and Due Care, are critical to upholding trust and public
confidence in the accountancy profession. The Misconduct also involved
widespread failures to comply with important auditing and quality control
standards, which are of fundamental importance to the work of an auditor.
g. Following Ms Nightingale’s departure from BDO in December 2019, the firm
conducted an extensive forensic investigation into, and collated information
relating to, her conduct and provided a detailed report on its findings to the
FRC in February 2021. The firm provided the FRC with its subsequent root
cause analysis later in 2021. BDO has remediated and strengthened its
systems and controls to try to prevent a reoccurrence of the Misconduct in the
future. However, since the Misconduct occurred, ‘quality control’ is an area
which the FRC has repeatedly found in its Audit Quality and Inspection Reports
to have contributed to findings that BDO’s audits have required improvement
or significant improvements.
h. The Misconduct is very likely to undermine confidence in the standards of
conduct in general of Members and Member Firms and financial reporting, and
in the profession generally.

4
Identification of Sanction
12. Having assessed the seriousness of the Misconduct and considered the range of
available sanctions, the Executive Counsel considers that the sanctions identified
at paragraph 9 above are appropriate.
13. The Executive Counsel considers that, having regard to the circumstances of this
case and the nature of the Misconduct and circumstances in which it has arisen,
a financial sanction of £6,500,000 is proportionate to the Misconduct and will act
as an effective deterrent.

14. In relation to those audits where unauthorised auditor’s reports were issued by the
firm, BDO has written (or, in relation to two audited entities, will write as soon as
practicable) to all extant audited entities where audit fees were charged, and
offered to repay those fees. BDO has repaid 6 audit fees and will take all
reasonable steps to repay fees, where charged, in relation to the remaining audits
within a period of 56 days, and report to the FRC on those steps following the
expiry of that period.

15. The Executive Counsel has determined it is also appropriate to impose a Severe
Reprimand given the scale and gravity of the Misconduct identified.
16. Further, the Executive Counsel has determined that BDO should undertake the
steps set out in the Schedule to this Agreement by way of Non-Financial
Sanctions.
17. The Executive Counsel has taken into account aggravating and mitigating factors
set out below, to the extent that they have not already been taken into account in
relation to the nature and seriousness of the Misconduct. The Executive Counsel
has also considered whether any adjustment to sanction for deterrence is required
in this case. The conclusion reached is that no adjustment is required.
Aggravating Factors
18. No other aggravating factors which have not already been taken into account in
the assessment of seriousness have been identified.
Mitigating Factors
19. BDO has expressed contrition for the Misconduct.
Discount for Settlement
20. Having taken into account the admissions made by BDO and the stage at which
those admissions were made (in Stage 3 of the case in accordance with paragraph

5
73 of the 2021 Sanctions Guidance), the Executive Counsel has determined that
a reduction of 10% to the financial sanction is appropriate.
Costs
21. Costs of £716,000 to be paid by BDO no later than 28 days after the date when
this Agreement takes effect.

[Signature redacted]

Jamie Symington

Date
Deputy Executive Counsel

[Signature redacted]
Mark Shaw

Date
8/8/2025
Partner, BDO LLP

[Signature redacted]
Gervase MacGregor

Date
08-08-25 | 13:12 BST
Partner, BDO LLP

6
Schedule to the Agreement
Non-Financial Sanctions
1. BDO to report to the FRC’s Executive Counsel and Executive Director of Supervision
every six months (on or before 31 May and 30 November based on data up to 31
March and 30 September respectively) for a period of two years (with the first report
to be provided on or before 31 May 2026 and the final report to be provided on or
before 30 November 2027) in respect of:

a. BDO’s monitoring and the results thereof, in respect of the implementation and
operating effectiveness of the six control enhancements set out below1, and of
any related measures introduced since December 2019, or remedial actions
taken in response to the firm’s monitoring.
i.
Use of Docusign (Electronic Signatures);
ii.
Scrape of Information from Companies House to confirm signatures on audit
reports;
iii. Logging and tracking opinions signed by Rls;
iv. Controls over handovers of portfolios;
v.
Controls in respect of WIP and debtors, including those intended to ensure
appropriate RI oversight, approval and scrutiny of WIP, billing, recoveries
and write-offs; and
vi. AQI and milestones dashboard, and controls over delegate sign-offs.
b. The operating effectiveness of BDO’s systems and controls as incorporated in
the ISQM (UK) 1 framework for ensuring appropriate involvement in, and
supervision of audits by RIs.

2. In reporting on the matters at 1(b) above, BDO’s reports should include:

a. Qualitative analysis of the systems and controls relevant to ensuring appropriate
involvement in, and supervision of audits by RIs, during the relevant reporting
period, including a summary of any potential deficiencies identified during that
period, which should include details of (insofar as relevant to those systems and
controls):

1 Such controls as have previously been reported to FRC Supervision by BDO

7
i.
The outcome of the firm-wide portfolio reviews (including the South East
SBU specific reviews);
ii.
A summary of any findings and interventions by the Audit Quality Executive;
and
iii. A summary of practice review findings for the relevant reporting period, and
of BDO’s actions in response to those findings.

3. BDO shall also include in its six-monthly reporting:

a. An anonymised breakdown of annual quality ratings for client-facing directors
and partners working within the audit practice including a summary of the actions
taken to improve performance where necessary;

b. An anonymised summary of disciplinary investigations undertaken under BDO’s
Disciplinary Policy for employees and equivalent policies/rules for partners, and
any sanctions applied, for the relevant reporting period in respect of client-facing
partners and qualified staff working within the audit practice;

c. An anonymised summary of external written complaints from audited entities
submitted to BDO’s risk reporting system for the relevant reporting period relating
to the audit practice, and how these were resolved; and

d. Any other information relevant to the operation of the relevant systems and
controls which the FRC would reasonably expect notice in the context of these
non-financial sanctions.

4. BDO’s reports will be signed by an appropriate member of Senior Management (to
be agreed with FRC) and will set out a description of the work that has been carried
out in preparing each report and the basis of the conclusions contained within each
report.

title: Sanctions against Amanda Nightingale (née Cleaver)
text:
1
Edited for publication
WITHOUT PREJUDICE
IN THE MATTER OF
THE EXECUTIVE COUNSEL TO THE FINANCIAL REPORTING COUNCIL
-and-
AMANDA NIGHTINGALE (NÉE CLEAVER)

SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT

The Settlement Agreement (which includes the Particulars of Fact and Acts of Misconduct) is a
document agreed between Amanda Nightingale and the Executive Counsel. It does not make
findings against any persons other than Ms Nightingale and it would not be fair to treat any
part of this document as constituting findings against any other persons.
1. This Settlement Agreement (“Agreement”) is made on 11 June 2024 between Jamie
Symington as Deputy Executive Counsel of the Financial Reporting Council (“the
Executive Counsel”), and Ms Amanda Nightingale (together “the Parties”). The
Agreement is evidenced by the signatures of the Parties.
2. The Parties recognise that the determination to be made in this case is a matter for the
Tribunal member in accordance with paragraph 8(4)(ii) of the FRC Accountancy
Scheme (“the Scheme”).
3. Terms used in this Agreement shall have the same meaning as set out in the Scheme
and the FRC Sanctions Guidance dated March 2021 (“the 2021 Sanctions
Guidance”).
4. If the decision is to approve the Agreement, including the sanctions set out below, then
the Agreement shall take effect from the next working day after the date on which the
notice of the decision is sent to the Parties in accordance with paragraph 8(4)(iv) of
the Scheme.

5. The Particulars of Fact and Acts of Misconduct against Amanda Nightingale ("the
Particulars”) as a former member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England
and Wales (“ICAEW”) were prepared by the Executive Counsel and agreed by the
Parties in accordance with the Scheme and are annexed at Annex 1.
6. The Particulars are in respect of Ms Nightingale’s conduct whilst employed by BDO
LLP as a Senior Manager. On numerous occasions between 2015 and 2019, the

2
conduct of Ms Nightingale fell significantly short of the standards reasonably to be
expected of a Member and has brought, or is likely to bring, discredit to herself, BDO
and to the accountancy profession in that she:
a. caused or permitted auditor’s reports to be issued without approval from the
Responsible Individuals, including by inserting electronic copies of the signature of
the Responsible Individual for the relevant audit without their authorisation;
b. inserted electronic copies of the signatures of the Responsible Individuals in other
documents, including company accounts which she then filed at Companies
House, without their authorisation;
c. created false documents, and falsified existing documents, including audit
evidence; and
d. deceived the Responsible Individuals and audited entities.
7. Ms Nightingale admits the Particulars and the 49 Allegations contained within it.
Sanction
8. The Parties have agreed the following terms of settlement in respect of sanction for
Ms Nightingale’s Misconduct:

a. Ms Nightingale be excluded from the ICAEW for a recommended period of 20
years;
b. A Condition that Ms Nightingale shall not undertake any accountancy work for a
period of 20 years, defined as:

acting as a “professional accountant in public practice” or a “professional
accountant in business” as defined in the glossary of the ICAEW Code of
Ethics1;

the matters defined as “public practice” by the ICAEW ‘Definition of public
practice’ guidance2;

being involved in preparing or signing financial statements, save as they relate
solely to her personal financial affairs;

performing any financial roles in the operation of a business, including but not
limited to: Chief Financial Officer, Finance Director, Group Finance Director,
Financial Controller, Finance Manager, Divisional Director of Finance; and

holding herself out as a member of the ICAEW, or as a person capable of
carrying out the above-listed accountancy work.

c. a published statement, in the form of a Severe Reprimand

1 See definition in Annex 1 and https://www.icaew.com/-/media/corporate/files/members/regulations-
standards-and-guidance/ethics/icaew-code-of-ethics-2020.ashx?la=en#page=193
2 See definition in Annex 2 and https://www.icaew.com/technical/practice-resources/regulations-standards-
guidance-and-ethics/definition-of-public-practice

3
9. In determining the appropriate sanctions against Ms Nightingale, the Executive
Counsel adopted the approach set out in paragraph 18 of the 2021 Sanctions
Guidance, as follows:

Nature and Seriousness of the Misconduct
10. The Executive Counsel considers that the factors relevant to assessing the nature and
seriousness of the Misconduct are:
a. The Misconduct in this case was of a very serious nature and involved forgery of
audit reports, the creation of false documents, falsifying existing documents and
deception of Responsible Individuals and audited entities.
b. The Misconduct involved a failure to comply with important professional standards.
The standards breached, including the Fundamental Principles of Integrity and
Professional Behaviour, are critical to upholding trust and public confidence in the
accountancy profession. The Misconduct also involved a failure to comply with the
requirements of s503 of the Companies Act 2006, which is further damaging to
public confidence in statutory audit.
c. The Misconduct was intentional and dishonest but it does not appear that any
financial gain was derived or intended to be derived from the Misconduct other than
her remuneration from BDO for performing professional services which she did not
perform to the required standard as detailed in the Particulars. The motivation for
the Misconduct remains unclear but certain of Ms Nightingale’s personal
circumstances have been taken into account as set out in the mitigating factors.
d. The scale and significance of the Misconduct was substantial. It was repeated on
numerous occasions, across numerous audits and occurred over a number of
years.
e. The Misconduct is likely to undermine confidence in the standards of conduct in
general of Members and Member Firms and financial reporting and in the
profession generally.
f. It is not alleged that the Misconduct caused or risked the loss of significant sums
of money or adversely affected or potentially adversely affected a significant
number of people in the United Kingdom given the nature and size of the audited
entities to which it relates.
g. The Executive Counsel cannot be confident that the same type of Misconduct will
not recur absent Ms Nightingale’s exclusion from the ICAEW and a Condition that
she does not undertake accountancy work for a very significant period.
Identification of Sanction

11. Having assessed the seriousness of the Misconduct and considered the range of
available sanctions, the Executive Counsel considers that the sanctions identified
above are appropriate.

4
12. Pursuant to paragraph 51 of the 2021 Sanctions Guidance, the Executive Counsel
considers that Exclusion from the ICAEW and the Condition not to undertake
accountancy work are necessary. The removal of Ms Nightingale’s professional status
is the most appropriate outcome in order to protect the public and safeguard the public
interest in circumstances where the Misconduct is so damaging to the wider public and
market confidence in the standards of conducts of Members and in the accountancy
profession.
13. For the avoidance of doubt, the Executive Counsel has considered all other available
sanctions and whether an Exclusion and the Condition are the most appropriate
sanctions and has concluded that they are given, among other things, the Misconduct
in this case is fundamentally incompatible with continued membership of the ICAEW
and the undertaking of accountancy work.
14. Further, the Executive Counsel has determined it is also appropriate to impose a
Severe Reprimand given the scale and gravity of the Misconduct identified.
15. The Executive Counsel has determined that it is not necessary to impose a financial
sanction in this matter having had regard to the factors listed at paragraph 33 of the
2021 Sanctions Guidance. Namely, Ms Nightingale does not appear to have derived
any financial gain or benefit as a result of the Misconduct, the Misconduct does not
appear to have involved or caused the loss of significant sums of money and, in view
of the unique and unprecedented nature of the Misconduct, there are no obvious
similar previous cases where a Fine was imposed.
16. Further, the Executive Counsel considers that the aims and objectives of the Scheme
and of sanctions as set out in paragraph 9 of the 2021 Sanctions Guidance can be
fulfilled without the imposition of a financial sanction. The Executive Counsel considers
that the exceptional period of Exclusion imposed on Ms Nightingale, together with the
onerous terms of the Condition and the Severe Reprimand are very grave sanctions,
the personal and financial effects of which will be very significant. Taking the package
of sanctions as a whole, Executive Counsel considers that they will declare and uphold
proper standards among Members, maintain and promote public and market
confidence in the accountancy profession, appropriately protect the public and act as
a sufficient deterrent.
17. The Executive Counsel has taken into account aggravating and mitigating factors as
set out below. The Executive Counsel has concluded that the sanctions set out in
paragraph 8 above are appropriate, and no adjustment to sanctions is necessary,
having regard to the purpose of the Scheme.
18. Further, having regard to paragraph 72 of the 2021 Sanctions Guidance, which states
that it will not normally be inappropriate to reduce the period which a Member is to be
precluded from practising to reflect a settlement because the primary purpose of such
a sanction is to protect the public, the Executive Counsel has concluded no discount
for settlement is appropriate.
Aggravating Factors

5
19. No aggravating factors which have not already been taken into account in the
assessment of seriousness have been identified.
Mitigating Factors
20. The following mitigating factors were identified:

a. Ms Nightingale has personal mitigating circumstances in that a close family
member suffered serious ill-health throughout the material period and that, in
conjunction with her full-time role as a senior manager in a large audit firm, this
placed very significant mental and physical burdens upon her.

b. Ms Nightingale has apologised and shown contrition for the Misconduct.
Deterrence
21. The Executive Counsel does not consider that an adjustment for deterrence is
required.
Costs
22. Having regard Ms Nightingale’s financial position Executive Counsel has determined
that she should make a contribution of £10,000 to the costs of this matter.

[11 June 2024]
…………………………………………..

………………………………..
Jamie Symington

Date
Deputy Executive Counsel

[redacted]

[10 June 2024]
…………………………………………..

………………………………..
