6.37. Paragraph 69 of the Sanctions Policy provides that:
“In order for cooperation to be considered as a mitigating factor at the point of
determining appropriate sanction it will therefore be necessary for the Statutory Auditors
and Statutory Audit Firms to have provided an exceptional level of cooperation. Non-
exhaustive examples of conduct which may constitute such cooperation include: a) self-
reporting to the FRC and/or bringing to the attention of the FRC any facts and/or matters
which may constitute an allegation of a breach of the Relevant Requirements…”
6.38. The Respondents provided an exceptional level of cooperation during the investigation.
In summary:
6.38.1. KPMG proactively investigated the concerns raised by Firm Y in FY22
regarding compliance with the 2019 Ethical Standard. KPMG prepared a Root
Cause Analysis document and offered to provide it to Executive Counsel (albeit
this was not ultimately necessary).
6.38.2. Promptly upon realising that the 2019 Ethical Standard had been breached in
relation to KAP rotation, and the provision of prohibited accounting services,
KPMG self-reported those breaches to their FRC Supervisor, and to Executive
Counsel’s case team.

31
OFFICIAL
6.38.3. During the investigation, KPMG (with Executive Counsel’s approval) undertook
its own enquiries of Firm X to establish the nature of the tax services provided,
and upon realising that the 2019 Ethical Standard had been breached in relation
to the provision of such services, KPMG self-reported those breaches to their
FRC Supervisor, and to Executive Counsel’s case team.
6.38.4. In responses to AEP Notices issued by Executive Counsel’s case team, the
Respondents volunteered additional information which had not been
specifically requested, in order to advance the case team’s understanding of
the facts. This conduct advanced the speed of the investigation.
6.38.5. In order to assist with Executive Counsel’s case team’s analysis, the
Respondents voluntarily provided information outside of the scope of the case
team’s requests.
6.38.6. The Respondents have shown a commendable level of transparency
throughout the investigation, including a notifying Executive Counsel of a
potential non-audit services issue on an unrelated Statutory Audit matter.
6.39. Whilst not amounting to exceptional cooperation, all of the Respondents’ responses to
AEP Notices were on time, full and complete.
6.40. In light of the Respondent’s exceptional cooperation, Executive Counsel considers that
a discount to the financial sanction of 15% is appropriate.
Other considerations
6.41. In accordance with paragraph 47(c) of the Sanctions Policy, Executive Counsel has
taken into account the financial resources and financial strength of the Respondents,
the effect of a financial Sanction on them, and whether they are insured (or otherwise
indemnified) as to any financial Sanction.
Deterrence
6.42. Having considered the matters set out at paragraphs 72 and 73 of the Sanctions Policy,
Executive Counsel considers that no adjustment for deterrence is required in this case.

Discount for Admissions and Settlement
6.43. Having taken into account the full admissions by the Respondents and the stage at
which those admissions were made (early in Stage 1 of the case in accordance with
paragraph 84 of the Sanctions Policy), Executive Counsel determines that a reduction
of 35% to the financial sanction is appropriate. This reflects the early stage at which the

32
OFFICIAL
Respondents made admissions (broadly, within nine months of the opening of the case),
their prompt and transparent engagement with Without Prejudice discussions and the
efficient disposal of this matter by way of a Final Settlement Decision Notice.
6.44. The effect of the combination of this discount, and the discount for exceptional
cooperation is that the following financial Sanctions are payable:
6.44.1. KPMG - £690,625; and
6.44.2. Mr Plumb - £38,675.

7.
COSTS
7.1. Additionally, Executive Counsel requires that the Respondents pay her costs in full in
this matter, being £219,755. Such costs shall be paid no later than 28 days after the
date of this Final Settlement Decision Notice.

Signed:
[Redacted.]
Jamie Symington

DEPUTY EXECUTIVE COUNSEL

Date: 25 February 2025

33
OFFICIAL
Appendix 1: Relevant Requirements

1.
The Relevant Requirements referred to in this Final Settlement Decision Notice are the
following.

The 2019 Ethical Standard

2.
Paragraph 1.47:
“In order to use the work of another firm (including network firms) for the purpose of an
engagement, the lead firm for the engagement has to obtain sufficient appropriate
evidence and be satisfied that such another firm is independent of each entity relevant
to the engagement in accordance with supporting ethical provision 2.4 of this Ethical
Standard”.

3.
Paragraph A2.4:
“For each engagement, the firm and the engagement partner (in the case of the
engagement partner insofar as they are able to do so) shall ensure that the firm’s
independence is not compromised as a result of conditions or relationships that would
compromise the independence of a network firm (whether or not its work is used in the
conduct of the engagement) or an other firm whose work is used in the conduct of the
engagement, having regard to the ethical requirements in this Ethical Standard that are
relevant to the engagement.”

4.
Paragraph 3.10:
“Save where the circumstances in paragraphs 3.14 and 3.15 apply, the key audit
partners responsible for carrying out a statutory audit of a public interest entity shall
cease their participation in the statutory audit of the audited entity not later than five
years from the date of their appointment. They shall not participate again in the statutory
audit of the audited entity before five years have elapsed following that cessation. This
includes time spent participating in an engagement, where an audit engagement has
moved between firms.”

5.
A footnote to paragraph 3.10 states that “For an audit, the engagement partner is a key
audit partner.”

6.
Paragraph 5.71:

34
OFFICIAL
“Where an entity relevant to the engagement is a listed entity, or a significant affiliate of
such an entity, the firm shall not provide a service to prepare current or deferred tax
calculations that are or may reasonably be expected to be used by the entity when
preparing accounting entries.”

7.
Paragraph 5.120:
“The firm shall not provide accounting services to an entity relevant to an engagement
where: (a) the entity is a listed entity, relevant to an engagement by the firm, or a
significant affiliate of such an entity...”

8.
The term “accounting services” in paragraph 5.120 is defined in paragraph 5.117 of the
2019 Ethical Standard:
“For the purpose of this Ethical Standard, the term ‘accounting services’ is defined as
the provision of services that involve the maintenance of accounting records or the
preparation of financial statements or other subject matter information or subject matter
that are then subject to audit or an other public interest assurance engagement. Advice
on the implementation of current and proposed accounting standards is not included in
the term accounting services”.

ISA 600
9.
ISA 600.11:
“The group engagement partner is responsible for the direction, supervision and
performance of the group audit engagement in compliance with professional standards
and applicable legal and regulatory requirements, and whether the auditor’s report that
is issued is appropriate in the circumstances. As a result, the auditor’s report on the
group financial statements shall not refer to a component auditor, unless required by law
or regulation to include such reference. If such reference is required by law or regulation,
the auditor’s report shall indicate that the reference does not diminish the group
engagement partner’s or the group engagement partner’s firm’s responsibility for the
group audit opinion.”

10.
ISA 600.19(a):
“If the group engagement team plans to request a component auditor to perform work
on the financial information of a component, the group engagement team shall obtain
an understanding of the following: (Ref: Para. A32–A35) (a) Whether the component

35
OFFICIAL
auditor understands and will comply with the ethical requirements that are relevant to
the group audit and, in particular, is independent. (Ref: Para. A37–A37-1)”.

11.
ISA 600.42:
“The group engagement team shall evaluate the component auditor’s communication
(see paragraph 41). The group engagement team shall: (a) Discuss significant matters
arising from that evaluation with the component auditor, component management or
group management, as appropriate; and (b) Determine whether it is necessary to review
other relevant parts of the component auditor’s audit documentation. (Ref: Para. A61)”.

title: Sanctions against Sean Robert Clark in relation to the operations and investment activities of Thurrock Council
text:
Edited for publication
IN THE MATTER OF:

THE EXECUTIVE COUNSEL TO THE FINANCIAL REPORTING COUNCIL

- and -

SEAN ROBERT CLARK

SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT

The Settlement Agreement (which includes the Particulars of Fact and Acts of
Misconduct) is a document agreed between Sean Robert Clark and the
Executive Counsel. It does not make findings against any persons or entities
other than Mr Clark and it would not be fair to treat any part of this document
as constituting or evidencing an investigation into, or findings in respect of
the conduct of, any other persons or entities.

1. This Settlement Agreement (“Agreement”) is made on the
[6th]
day of
November 2024 between Claudia Mortimore, Deputy Executive Counsel of the
Financial Reporting Council (“FRC”), of 8th Floor, 125 London Wall, London,
EC2Y 5AS (“the Executive Counsel”) and Sean Robert Clark (“Mr Clark”). The
Executive Counsel and Mr Clark together are described as “the Parties”.
2. The Agreement is evidenced by the signatures of the Executive Counsel and by
Mr Clark.
3. The Particulars of Fact and Acts of Misconduct (“the Particulars”) concerning
the actions of Mr Clark as a Member of the Association of Chartered Certified

2
Accountants (“ACCA”) annexed to this Agreement were prepared by Executive
Counsel in accordance with the Accountancy Scheme of 1 January 2021,
reissued on 30 March 2021 (“the Scheme”).
4. The Particulars concern the conduct of Mr Clark in relation to the operations and
investment activities of Thurrock Council (“the Council”) for the financial years
ended 31 March 2018 to 31 March 2022, and specifically the implementation by
him of a “debt for yield” approach by which the Council borrowed large sums of
money on a short-term basis and used it to make longer-term investments, some
of which failed.
5. As set out in detail in the Particulars, the conduct of Mr Clark fell significantly
short of the standards reasonably to be expected of him in that he:
a. Failed to comply with restrictions on the exercise of delegated authority;
b. Failed to comply with the relevant statutory framework in implementing
the “debt for yield” approach;
c. Failed to ensure that the Council had access to the necessary skills and
experience to pursue its “debt for yield” approach;
d. Failed adequately to manage and report on the risks arising from the
“debt for yield” approach; and
e. Recklessly provided misleading information about the “debt for yield”
approach (together, the “Acts of Misconduct”).
6. Mr Clark agrees the Particulars and admits the Acts of Misconduct in their
entirety.
7. The Parties recognise that it is for the Tribunal Panel member appointed under
paragraph 8(4)(i) of the Scheme to determine whether it would be appropriate for
this Agreement to be entered into, in accordance with paragraph 8(4)(ii) of the
Scheme.
Sanctions
8. The Parties agree the following sanctions:
a. Exclusion as a Member of the ACCA for a recommended period of 5
years.
b. A Severe Reprimand.

3
9. These sanctions have been determined in accordance with the approach set out
in the Accountancy Scheme Sanctions Guidance of March 2021 (the “Sanctions
Guidance”), as set out below.
Nature and Seriousness of the Misconduct
10. The following matters are relevant in assessing the nature and seriousness of
the Misconduct:
a. The Misconduct involved significant breaches of several fundamental
principles governing the conduct of accountants, namely the principles of
professional competence and due care, professional behaviour and
integrity.
b. Mr Clark held a senior position with supervisory responsibilities. He had
statutory responsibility for the administration of the Council’s financial
affairs, and was in a fiduciary position in respect of the public funds under
his control.
c. The Misconduct as a whole spanned a period of some five years,
although the allegation of lack of integrity concerned a much narrower
period of less than two months.
d. The Misconduct caused the loss of significant sums of money and
adversely affected the 176,000 residents in the Council area.
e. The Misconduct has undermined confidence in the standards of conduct
of Members in general and in the accounting profession generally.
f. The Misconduct was not dishonest or deliberate. It was not reckless,
except in the case of the reckless provision of misleading information,
which is reflected in the allegation of lack of integrity.
g. Mr Clark considered that he was acting in the best interests of the Council
and residents, in seeking to address a significant projected gap in
funding.
h. The Misconduct was not motivated by financial gain.
i.
A statutory Best Value Inspection of the Council found that there were
wider failings of leadership, governance and culture which allowed and
encouraged Mr Clark to act as he did.
j.
With exception of the admitted Acts of Misconduct in this matter, Mr Clark
has an unblemished record of 36 years of public service.

4
k. Mr Clark has already suffered significant financial and personal
consequences as a result of the events at the Council and the resulting
media attention.
Identification of Sanction
11. The Misconduct, taken as a whole, is so damaging to wider public confidence in
the standards of conduct of Members and in the profession that removal of
professional status is the appropriate outcome in order to protect the public or
otherwise safeguard the public interest.
12. Having regard to the seriousness of the Misconduct as summarised above,
exclusion from membership of the ACCA for a recommended period of 5 years
and a Severe Reprimand are the appropriate sanctions.
Aggravating and Mitigating Factors
13. The relevant aggravating and mitigating factors have already been identified and
taken into account when assessing the nature and seriousness of the
Misconduct.
Deterrence
14. No adjustment for deterrence is required in this case, in light of the sanctions to
be imposed.
Discount for Admissions and Settlement
15. While this Agreement was reached at Stage 1 of the disciplinary process (within
the meaning of paragraph 73 of the Sanctions Guidance), no discount for
settlement is appropriate, in light of the nature of the sanctions to be imposed.
Other Considerations
16. Having regard to Mr Clark’s existing financial resources and future employment
prospects, it would not be proportionate or necessary, in light of the aims and
objectives of the Scheme, to impose any fine. Neither would it be appropriate to
require Mr Clark to make any contribution towards the FRC’s costs.
Final matters
17. If the decision of the Tribunal Panel member is to approve this Agreement, then
the Agreement shall take effect from the next working day after the date on which
the notice of the decision is sent to Mr Clark in accordance with paragraph
8(4)(iv) of the Scheme.

5
18. The Agreement and Particulars will remain confidential until publication, in
accordance with paragraph 8(6) of the Scheme.

[redacted]

5 November 2024
Claudia Mortimore

Date
Deputy Executive Counsel

Sean Robert Clark

Date
[redacted]

title: Sanctions against Ernst & Young LLP and Mr Christopher Voogd
text:
IN THE MATTER OF
THE EXECUTIVE COUNSEL OF THE FINANCIAL REPORTING COUNCIL
-and-
(1) ERNST & YOUNG LLP

(2) MR CHRISTOPHER JULES VOOGD

FINAL SETTLEMENT DECISION NOTICE

Pursuant to Rule 108 of the Audit Enforcement Procedure

This Final Settlement Decision Notice is a document prepared by Executive Counsel
following an investigation relating to, and admissions made by, the Respondents. It
does not make findings against any persons or entities other than the Respondents
and it would not be fair to treat any part of this document as constituting or
evidencing findings against any other persons or entities since they are not parties to
the proceedings.
1.
INTRODUCTION
1.1. The Financial Reporting Council (the “FRC”) is the competent authority for Statutory
Audit in the UK and operates the Audit Enforcement Procedure (the “AEP”), revised in
June 2023. The AEP sets out the rules and procedure for the investigation, prosecution
and sanctioning of breaches of Relevant Requirements.
1.2. The AEP contains a number of defined terms and, for convenience, those defined terms
are also used within this document. Where terms defined in the AEP are used, they
appear in italics.
1.3. This Final Settlement Decision Notice also uses the following definitions:
1.3.1.
“FY2019” means the financial year ended 31 December 2019, “FY2019
financial statements” means the financial statements of Stirling Water

Page 2 of 26

Seafield Finance plc (“SWSF”) for that period, and “FY2019 Audit” means the
Statutory Audit of the FY2019 financial statements.
1.3.2.
“FY2009” means the financial year ended 31 March 2009, “FY2009 financial
statements” means SWSF’s financial statements for that period, and “FY2009
Audit” means the Statutory Audit of the FY2009 financial statements.
1.3.3.
“FY2018” means the financial year ended 31 December 2018, “FY2018
financial statements” means SWSF’s financial statements for that period, and
“FY2018 Audit” means the Statutory Audit of the FY2018 financial statements.
1.3.4.
“FY2020” means the financial year ended 31 December 2020, “FY2020
financial statements” means SWSF’s financial statements for that period, and
“FY2020 Audit” means the Statutory Audit of the FY2020 financial statements.
1.3.5.
“Respondents” means:
1.3.5.1. Ernst & Young LLP (“EY”) which was the Statutory Audit Firm for the
FY2019 Audit and all prior audits since the FY2009 Audit.
1.3.5.2. Mr Christopher Jules Voogd, who was the Statutory Auditor of SWSF
for the FY2019 Audit and signed the FY2019 Audit report on behalf of
EY.
1.4. In accordance with Rule 102 of the AEP, Executive Counsel entered into settlement
discussions with the Respondents. A Proposed Settlement Decision Notice was issued
by Executive Counsel on 18 November 2024 pursuant to Rule 103 of the AEP in relation
to the conduct of the Respondents in respect of the FY2019 Audit only. The
Respondents provided written agreement to the Proposed Settlement Decision Notice,
pursuant to Rule 105 of the AEP, on 25 November 2024.
1.5. The Convener subsequently appointed an Independent Reviewer, pursuant to Rule 106
of the AEP, to consider the Proposed Settlement Decision Notice. On 11 December
2024, the Independent Reviewer approved the issuance of this Final Settlement
Decision Notice pursuant to Rule 107(a) of the AEP.
1.6. In accordance with Rule 108 of the AEP, this Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out:
1.6.1.
the breaches of Relevant Requirement(s), with reasons;
1.6.2.
the Sanctions imposed on the Respondents, with reasons; and
1.6.3.
the amount payable by the Respondents in respect of Executive Counsel’s
Costs.
1.7. This Final Settlement Decision Notice is divided into the following sections:

Page 3 of 26

1.7.1.
Section 2: Executive Summary of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
1.7.2.
Section 3: Background;
1.7.3.
Section 4: Relevant Requirements to which the breaches relate;
1.7.4.
Section 5: Details of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
1.7.5.
Section 6: Sanctions; and
1.7.6.
Section 7: Costs.
2.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
2.1. SWSF is part of an international group of companies (the “Group”), the parent company
of which is headquartered in Europe. SWSF raises funds for other Group companies
and since 2002 it has had bonds admitted to trading on the Main Market of the London
Stock Exchange (“LSE”). As a result, since 2002 SWSF has been and remains a Public
Interest Entity (“PIE”) for the purposes of audit regulation.
2.2. Since 17 June 2016 the Companies Act 20061 has, in summary, imposed a “maximum
engagement period” of ten consecutive years for a Statutory Audit Firm so acting in
respect of a PIE, unless the Statutory Audit Firm was subsequently re-appointed during
that period following a public tender process. These provisions impose requirements,
commonly referred to as Mandatory Firm Rotation (“MFR”) requirements, which have
effect for financial years of companies beginning on or after 17 June 2016. The FRC’s
Revised Ethical Standard (“the Ethical Standard”) imposed a separate obligation to
comply with those requirements. By carrying out the FY2019 Audit, EY breached those
statutory provisions and the Ethical Standard, and both Respondents breached ISA (UK)
200 (Revised June 2016) (“ISA 200”) and ISA (UK) 220 (Revised June 2016) (Updated
July 2017) (“ISA 220”), in relation to the MFR requirements. It is not alleged that the
FY2019 Audit otherwise failed to meet Relevant Requirements or that the FY2019
financial statements were misstated.
2.3. The Companies Act 2006, as amended by the Statutory Auditors and Third Country
Auditors Regulations 2016 and 2017, gave effect to Article 17(1) of the EU Audit
Regulation2, which provided:
“Duration of the audit engagement

1 Sections 489C and 494ZA of the Companies Act 2006.
2 Regulation (EU) No. 537/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council dated 16 April 2014 (“the EU
Audit Regulation”)

Page 4 of 26

A public-interest entity shall appoint a statutory auditor or an audit firm for an initial
engagement of at least one year. The engagement may be renewed. Neither the initial
engagement of a particular statutory auditor or audit firm, nor this in combination with
any renewed engagements therewith shall exceed a maximum duration of 10 years.”
2.4. The purpose of the MFR requirement is to ensure the Statutory Audit Firm’s
independence, and the perception of independence, by either rotating off a PIE audit
engagement after ten years or taking part in a public tender to retain the audit. Recital
(21) to the EU Audit Regulation puts it as follows:
“In order to address the familiarity threat and therefore reinforce the independence of
statutory auditors and audit firms, it is important to establish a maximum duration of the
audit engagement of a statutory auditor or an audit firm in a particular audited entity. In
addition, as a means of strengthening the independence of the statutory auditor or the
audit firm, reinforcing professional scepticism, and increasing audit quality, this
Regulation provides for the following alternatives for an extension of the maximum
duration: regular and open mandatory retendering or the appointment of more than one
statutory auditor or audit firm by public-interest entities.”
2.5. In June 2016 the FRC published the Ethical Standard which included compliance with
the MFR requirements. Paragraph 3.9 of the Ethical Standard provided:
“Public Interest Entities and Other Listed Entities
Audit Firm Rotation
The requirements for audit firm rotation, implementing the relevant provisions of Article
17 of the EU Audit Regulation, are set out in legislation.3 The firm shall ensure that it
does not accept or continue an audit engagement that would cause those requirements
to not be complied with.”
2.6. MFR is a clear and well-known mandatory requirement enshrined in primary legislation
since 17 June 2016 through amendment to the Companies Act 2006. Furthermore, MFR
is an integral part of the ethical requirements to ensure auditor independence, and the
perception of independence, and is a key area of responsibility for a Statutory Auditor
which cannot be delegated.
2.7. As is set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice:

3 The Ethical Standard refers to sections 487 and 489 of the Companies Act 2006; the updated applicable
references are sections 489C and 494ZA.

Page 5 of 26

2.7.1.
EY was appointed auditor of SWSF for the FY2009 Audit without a public tender
process. It remained the Statutory Audit Firm of SWSF for all financial years up
to and including FY2019 without a public tender in any subsequent period.
2.7.2.
During the planning of the FY2020 Audit in early February 2021, EY identified
a potential breach of the MFR requirements, when the senior manager was
completing the continuance procedures for the FY2020 Audit. By the end of
April 2021 the Respondents concluded that they were in breach of the statutory
requirements for MFR, set out at paragraph 2.2 above, which meant that EY
should not have continued with the audit engagement of SWSF beyond
completion of the FY2018 Audit without having been re-appointed following a
public tender.
2.7.3.
EY resigned the engagement for the FY2020 Audit on 29 April 2021. It therefore
did not conduct the FY2020 Audit. EY informed the FRC of its resignation as
SWSF’s Statutory Audit Firm due to a breach of MFR requirements, on 30 April
2021, as it was required to do in accordance with the Companies Act 2006.
2.7.4.
When the Respondents subsequently reported further details of the ethical
breach to the FRC, on 4 November 2021, as part of EY’s bi-annual reporting
covering the period 1 April 2021 to 30 September 2021, they acknowledged
that by carrying out the FY2019 Audit, EY breached the maximum ten year
engagement period set out in the Companies Act 2006 and the Ethical
Standard. On 5 October 2022, before the FRC’s investigation into this matter
commenced, the Respondents provided the FRC’s Case Examiner with a copy
of an internal memorandum that EY had produced in May 2021 which detailed
the circumstances leading to the breach and identified the factors which in EY’s
view contributed to the breach.
2.7.5.
The FRC and EY have separately identified the following factors that
contributed to the breach occurring.
2.7.5.1. The lack of any centralised monitoring of MFR by EY.
2.7.5.2. EY’s internal electronic form that was used for acceptance and
continuance of each client engagement, was known as the Process
for Acceptance of Clients and Engagements (the “PACE” form). The
PACE form used for the FY2019 Audit (hereafter the “FY2019 PACE”)
contained multiple choice questions, one of which (question 2.2.1)
allowed the FY2019 Audit team to select (in error) an option which
stated that the MFR requirements did not apply to SWSF in FY2019,

Page 6 of 26

despite the FY2019 PACE showing that SWSF was a PIE and thus
automatically subject to MFR.
2.7.5.3. The failure by the FY2019 Audit team, including Mr Voogd, to notice
the error outlined at paragraph 2.7.5.2 above when approving the draft
PACE FY2019, despite question 2.2.1 specifically asking whether the
lead engagement partner, in this case Mr Voogd, had confirmed that
the firm was eligible for reappointment.
2.7.5.4. EY’s systems and processes allowed the FY2019 Audit team to
access, complete and upload an out-of-date version of the relevant
workpaper template when performing a separate independence
assessment (the “independence workpaper”), during the FY2019
Audit,
to
assess
EY’s
compliance
with
the
independence
requirements. That template did not contain questions regarding the
correct MFR requirements in force at the time of the FY2019 Audit.
2.7.5.5. The auditor’s report in the FY2019 financial statements, signed by Mr
Voogd, (and the auditor’s report in the FY2018 financial statements
signed by Mr Voogd’s predecessor4) disclosed a duration of EY’s audit
engagement that exceeded ten years. Neither Mr Voogd nor any other
member of the FY2019 Audit team challenged the compatibility of this
disclosure with the MFR requirements. Mr Voogd assumed
(incorrectly) that the issue of MFR had arisen and been resolved in
earlier years during which there had been a tender process at Group
level.
2.7.6.
Having identified and then reported this issue in 2021, EY has taken a number
of steps to prevent recurrence of a breach of the MFR requirements.
2.8. Section 5 of this Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out the detailed breaches of
Relevant Requirements.
2.9. This Final Settlement Decision Notice imposes the following Sanctions in respect of the
Respondents:

4 The audit report for the FY2018 financial statements identified that the period of total uninterrupted engagement
was 11 years, however, given the referenced change in accounting period, the total was in fact 10 years and 9
months. The breach occurred in relation to the FY2019 Audit, as opposed to the FY2018 Audit, as at 1 January
2018 (i.e. the first day of the financial year for the 2018 Audit) the engagement had not yet reached a duration of
10 years which runs from the start of the financial year for which the auditor was first appointed (which in this
case was 1 April 2008), as set out in section 494ZA of the Companies Act 2006.

Page 7 of 26

EY
2.9.1. a financial sanction of £500,000, adjusted for aggravating and mitigating
factors, and subject to a discount of 35% for admissions and early settlement so
that the financial sanction payable is £325,000;
2.9.2. a published statement in the form of a severe reprimand;
2.9.3. a declaration that the FY2019 Audit report signed on behalf of EY did not satisfy
the Relevant Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice;
and
2.9.4. an order, in the terms set down at Section 6 below, designed to prevent the
recurrence of the contravention
Mr Voogd
2.9.5. a financial sanction of £50,000, adjusted for aggravating and mitigating factors,
and subject to a discount of 35% for admissions and early settlement so that the
financial sanction payable is £32,500;
2.9.6. a published statement in the form of a severe reprimand; and
2.9.7. a declaration that the FY2019 Audit report signed by Mr Voogd did not satisfy
the Relevant Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice.
3.
BACKGROUND
3.1. In 2023, EY had audit fee income of £737 million, 132 audit principals and 216 PIE audit
clients.5 In 2019, EY had 252 PIE audit clients.6
3.2. Mr Voogd is a partner of EY. He was admitted as a member of the Institute of Chartered
Accountants of England and Wales in 1990 and has been a partner of EY since 1999.
Mr Voogd is an experienced Assurance Partner. He signed the FY2019 Audit report, on
behalf of EY, in respect of the FY2019 financial statements of SWSF on 23 April 2020.
FY2019 was Mr Voogd’s first year as Statutory Auditor for SWSF.
3.3. SWSF is a wholly owned subsidiary of a UK parent company, which is itself a wholly
owned subsidiary of a European parent company that at all material times was an audit
client of EY’s European audit entity. The FY2019 financial statements included the
following description of SWSF in the Directors’ Strategic Report:

5 Figure 33, pages 47-8, Key Facts and Trends in the Accountancy Profession 2024.
6 Figure 33, page 43, Key Facts and Trends in the Accountancy Profession 2020.

Page 8 of 26

“The principal activity of Stirling Water Seafield Finance plc (“the Company”) is to raise
funds to enable other UK&I group companies to upgrade and operate waste water
treatment facilities and provide services relating to the treatment and disposal of sewage
sludge in relation to the Almond Valley, Seafield and Esk (“AVSE”) catchment areas.
The Company is registered and domiciled in the United Kingdom.
The Company is part of the [international parent company group] (“the Group”) which is

BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
Breach 1 – Breach by EY of applicable statutory MFR requirements
EY breached section 489C of the Companies Act 2006, and thereby paragraph 3.9
of the Ethical Standard, by undertaking the FY2019 Audit.
5.1. As noted above, EY was required to comply with the Companies Act 2006 and the
Ethical Standard as regards MFR. The Companies Act 2006, (which gives effect to the
EU Audit Regulation), specifies a ten year maximum period for audit engagements of a
PIE, subject to exceptions explained in the following paragraph.8
5.2. Neither the Ethical Standard nor the statutory provisions set out above provide for
exceptions to the ten year period, save where a public tender is carried out during the
ten year period or, in exceptional circumstances, the maximum engagement period is
extended with the approval of the FRC. There can be no safeguards put in place to
mitigate the threats caused to independence by exceeding the “maximum engagement
period”.
5.3. The “maximum engagement period” is defined in section 494ZA of the Companies Act
2006. Applying that definition to EY’s audit of SWSF results in a maximum engagement
period that ends with “the last financial year of the company to begin within the period
of 10 years beginning with the first day of the first financial year of the maximum
engagement period”. On the facts of this case, the first day of the first financial year of
the maximum engagement period was 1 April 2008. The last financial year of the
company to begin within a period of ten years from 1 April 2008 was FY2018.
Accordingly, the maximum engagement period permitted, absent a public tender or
exceptional circumstances, ended with the completion of the FY2018 Audit.
5.4. EY breached section 489C of the Companies Act 2006 and paragraph 3.9 of the Ethical
Standard, by accepting its appointment as Statutory Auditor for FY2019 Audit.

June 2016) recognizes that the engagement team is entitled to rely on a firm’s system
of quality control in meeting its responsibilities with respect to quality control procedures
applicable to the individual audit engagement, unless information provided by the firm
or other parties suggests otherwise.”

ISA 220 (Quality Control for an Audit of Financial Statements)

5.
Paragraph 9 states:
“Throughout the audit engagement, the engagement partner shall remain alert,
through observation and making enquiries as necessary, for evidence of non-
compliance with relevant ethical requirements by members of the engagement team”.
(Ref: Para. A4-A5)

6.
Paragraph 11 states:
“The engagement partner shall form a conclusion on compliance with independence
requirements that apply to the audit engagement. In doing so, the engagement partner
shall (Ref: Para. A5)
(a) Obtain relevant information from the firm and, where appliable, network firms, to
identify and evaluate circumstances and relationships that create threats to
independence;
(b) Evaluate information on identified breaches, if any, of the firm's independence
policies and procedures to determine whether they create a threat to independence
for the audit engagement; and
(c) Take appropriate action to eliminate such threats or reduce them to an acceptable
level by applying safeguards, or, if considered appropriate, to withdraw from the
audit engagement, where withdrawal is possible under applicable law or regulation.
The engagement partner shall promptly report to the firm any inability to resolve
the matter for appropriate action.”

Page 24 of 26

7.
Paragraph 12 states:
“The engagement partner shall be satisfied that appropriate procedures regarding the
acceptance and continuance of client relationships and audit engagements have
been followed, and shall determine that conclusions reached in this regard are
appropriate. (Ref: Para. A8–A9)”
The guidance at paragraph A8 states (emphasis supplied):
“A8. ISQC (UK) 1 (Revised June 2016) requires the firm to obtain information
considered necessary in the circumstances before accepting an engagement with a
new client, when deciding whether to continue an existing engagement, and when
considering acceptance of a new engagement with an existing client. Information such
as the following assists the engagement partner in determining whether the
conclusions reached regarding the acceptance and continuance of client relationships
and audit engagements are appropriate:

The integrity of the principal owners, key management and those charged with
governance of the entity;

Whether the engagement team is competent to perform the audit engagement
and has the necessary capabilities, including time and resources;

Whether the firm and the engagement team can comply with relevant
ethical requirements; and

Significant matters that have arisen during the current or previous audit
engagement, and their implications for continuing the relationship.” (emphasis
added).
8.
Paragraph 15 states:
“The engagement partner shall take responsibility for:
(a) The direction, supervision and performance of the audit engagement in compliance
with professional standards and applicable legal and regulatory requirements (Ref:
Para A13-A15,A20); and
(b) The auditor’s report being appropriate in the circumstances”.

Page 25 of 26

Extracts from ISQC 1 (Quality Control for Firms that perform Audits and Reviews of Financial
Statements, and other Assurance and Related Services Engagements)

9.
Paragraphs 21 states:
“The firm shall establish policies and procedures designed to provide it with reasonable
assurance that the firm, its personnel and, where applicable, others subject to
independence requirements … maintain independence where required by relevant
ethical requirements”
10.
Paragraph 22(c)(i) states:
“Such policies and procedures shall require ..(c) the accumulation and communication
of relevant information to appropriate personnel so that (i) the firm and its personnel can
readily determine whether they satisfy independence requirements”.
11.
Paragraph 27R-2(b) states:
“Before accepting or continuing an engagement for an audit engagement of a public
interest entity .. the firm shall also assess the following:
(b) whether the conditions for the duration of the audit engagement in
accordance with UK law are complied with”.

Extracts from the Ethical Standard

12.
Paragraph I9 provides:
“Part A of this Ethical Standard sets out the overarching principles of integrity, objectivity
and independence, together with supporting ethical provisions. Together, these
establish a framework, of ethical outcomes that are required to be met by the auditor or
assurance practitioner, to provide a basis for user trust and confidence in the integrity
and objectivity of the practitioner in performing the engagement.”
13.
Paragraph 1.10 provides:
“The senior management of the firm, and those with direct responsibility for the
management of the firm’s audit and other public interest assurance business, shall
establish appropriate policies, procedures and quality control and monitoring systems;
dedicate appropriate resources and leadership to compliance with supporting ethical
provision 1.1; and make appropriate arrangements with network firms to ensure

Page 26 of 26

compliance as necessary across the network. The firm shall ensure that such
appropriate policies, procedures and quality control and monitoring systems are
implemented and operated effectively.”
14.
Paragraph 3.9 provides:
“Public Interest Entities and Other Listed Entities
Audit Firm Rotation
The requirements for audit firm rotation, implementing the relevant provisions of Article
17 of the EU Audit Regulation, are set out in legislation. The firm shall ensure that it
does not accept or continue an audit engagement that would cause those requirements
to not be complied with.”

title: Sanctions against Ernst & Young LLP and Richard Wilson
text:
Edited for Publication
IN THE MATTER OF

THE EXECUTIVE COUNSEL TO THE FINANCIAL REPORTING COUNCIL

-and-

(1) ERNST & YOUNG LLP
(2) MR RICHARD WILSON

FINAL SETTLEMENT DECISION NOTICE
Pursuant to Rule 108 of the Audit Enforcement Procedure

This Final Settlement Decision Notice is a document prepared by Executive Counsel
following an investigation relating to the Respondents. It does not make findings
against any persons or entities other than the Respondents and it would not be fair to
treat any part of this document as constituting or evidencing findings against any other
persons or entities since they are not parties to the proceedings.

2
1.
INTRODUCTION
1.1
The Financial Reporting Council (the “FRC”) is the competent authority for Statutory
Audit in the United Kingdom and operates the Audit Enforcement Procedure (the
“AEP”), revised in June 2023. The AEP sets out the rules and procedure for the
investigation, prosecution and sanctioning of breaches of “Relevant Requirements”.
1.2
The AEP contains a number of defined terms and, for convenience, those defined
terms are also used within this document. Where defined terms are used, they appear
in italics.
1.3
This Final Settlement Decision Notice also uses the following definitions:
(i)
“Applicable
Accounting
Framework”
means
the
International
Accounting Standards (“IAS”) or International Financial Reporting
Standards (“IFRS”) as applicable.
(ii)
“Audit Team” means Mr Richard Wilson (as the Statutory Auditor) and
other EY staff who performed audit procedures on either the FY17 Audit
or the FY18 Audit where relevant. For the FY18 Audit the Audit Team also
included members of EY’s Restructuring Department (to which see
paragraph 2.17 below).
(iii) “the Company” means Thomas Cook Group Plc, the ultimate holding
company of the Group.
(iv) “the Group” or “Thomas Cook” means the group of companies owned
and/or operated by the Company (including the Company itself).
(v)
“Ethical Standard 2016” means the Revised Ethical Standard 2016
issued by the FRC.
(vi) “FY17” means the financial year ended 30 September 2017.
(vii) “FY18” means the financial year ended 30 September 2018.
(viii) “FY17 Financial Statements” means the consolidated financial
statements of the Group for FY17 signed on 21 November 2017.

3
(ix) “FY18 Financial Statements” means the consolidated financial
statements of the Group for FY18 approved for issue on 28 November
2018.
(x)
“FY17 Audit” means the Statutory Audit of the FY17 Financial Statements.
(xi) “FY18 Audit” means the Statutory Audit of the FY18 Financial Statements.
(xii) “Relevant Time” means the period covering the FY17 and FY18 Audits.
1.4
This Final Settlement Decision Notice is issued pursuant to Rule 108 of the AEP in
respect of the conduct of:
(i)
Ernst & Young LLP (“EY”) the Statutory Audit Firm of the Group for the
FY17 and FY18 Audits.
(ii)
Mr Richard Wilson (“Mr Wilson”) a partner in EY at the Relevant Time and
the Statutory Auditor responsible for the FY17 and FY18 Audits. Mr Wilson
signed the FY17 and FY18 Audit Reports1 on behalf of EY.
1.5
In this Final Settlement Decision Notice, EY and Mr Wilson are referred to as the
“Respondents”.
1.6
In accordance with Rule 102 of the AEP, Executive Counsel entered into settlement
discussions with the Respondents.
1.7
A Proposed Settlement Decision Notice was issued by Executive Counsel on 11
November 2024 pursuant to Rule 103 of the AEP in relation to the conduct of the
Respondents in respect of the FY17 and FY18 Audits. The Respondents provided
written agreement to the Proposed Settlement Decision Notice, pursuant to Rule 105
of the AEP, on 27 November 2024. The Convener subsequently appointed an
Independent Reviewer, pursuant to Rule 106 of the AEP, to consider the Proposed
Settlement Decision Notice.
1.8
On 17 December 2024, the Independent Reviewer approved the issuance of this
Final Settlement Decision Notice pursuant to Rule 107(a) of the AEP.

1
As defined at paragraphs 2.8 and 2.20 below.

4
1.9
In accordance with Rule 108 of the AEP this Final Settlement Decision Notice sets
out:
(i)
the breaches of Relevant Requirement(s), with reasons;
(ii)
the Sanctions imposed on the Respondents with reasons; and
(iii) the amount payable by the Respondents in respect of Executive Counsel’s
Costs.
1.10
This Final Settlement Decision Notice is divided into the following sections:
(i)
Section 2: Background;
(ii)
Section 3: Executive Summary of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
(iii) Section 4: Relevant Requirements to which the breaches relate;
(iv) Section 5: Detail of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
(v)
Section 6: Sanctions;
(vi) Section 7: Costs.

5
2.
BACKGROUND
2.1
The Group described itself as “one of the world’s leading travel groups”2 (comprising
traditional travel agent services and an airline) and, as at September 2019, operated
from 16 countries, with 21,000 employees. The Company’s shares were listed on the
main market of the London Stock Exchange.
2.2
In 2011, the Group suffered a loss in bookings which was attributed to disruption in
the Middle East/African region. The Group required an additional £200 million loan
from its bankers to fund a shortfall in cashflow.
2.3
In 2012/2013 the Group commenced a transformation project to reform the business
and move it towards profitable growth. In 2015, the Group refinanced its existing
borrowings.
2.4
In 2016, the Group suffered a fall in bookings which was attributed to overseas
terrorist attacks in the previous year3.
FY17
2.5
FY17 was EY’s first year of auditing Thomas Cook.
2.6
The FY17 Financial Statements were signed on 21 November 2017. The Group
Income Statement reported revenue of £9.007 billion, gross profit of £1.993 billion
and profit after tax for the year of £12 million. The Company’s Group Balance Sheet
reported total assets of £6.615 billion, total liabilities of £6.335 billion, and therefore
net assets of £280 million. Audit materiality was set at £15 million.
2.7
The FY17 Financial Statements accounted for £2.6 billion of Goodwill. This
represented 40% of the Group’s total assets and was the largest single item on the
balance sheet. As a result, a misstatement in the Goodwill balance had the potential
to be very large (as the Audit Team appreciated). Goodwill was not subject to any
impairment in FY17.
2.8
The FY17 Independent Auditor’s Report (“FY17 Audit Report”) signed by Mr Wilson
was unmodified. The FY17 Audit Report disclosed the carrying value of Goodwill as

2
As described in the FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements.
3 Report by the Official Receiver on the Thomas Cook Group companies:
(https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/85
2083/Thomas_Cook_report_to_creditors_and_contributories.pdf)

6
a ‘Key Audit Matter’. It was included as a “significant issue[s] in relation to the financial
statements” that was considered by the Audit Committee in the FY17 Corporate
Governance Report, although it was not treated as a significant audit risk by the
Respondents.

2.9
Note 12 to the FY17 Financial Statements included disclosures about Goodwill and
the impairment testing of Goodwill by Thomas Cook. The note explained that
impairment testing was performed by comparing the carrying value of each cash-
generating unit (“CGU”) to the recoverable amount, determined on the basis of the
CGU’s Value In Use (“VIU”). In summary, this involved comparing the value attributed
to the CGU’s assets to the future cashflows expected to be derived from using those
assets.
2.10
The Group divided its business into four CGUs for this purpose (which were also
adopted as its operating segments for the purpose of segmental reporting4). These
CGUs were UK Tour Operator (“UKTO”); Northern Europe Tour Operator (“NETO”);
Continental Tour Operator (“CETO”); and Group Airlines (“GAS”). The FY17 Financial
Statements were the first occasion on which these CGUs were adopted for the
Group’s financial reporting.
2.11
Note 4 to the FY17 Financial Statements explained that during the year the Group
had refined its organisational structure, resulting in a reassessment of its reportable
segments. Previous financial statements had reported segments on a geographical
basis (UK, Northern Europe, Continental Europe and Condor5). The major change
effected by the re-organisation was that the Group’s airline business was treated as
a separate CGU from FY17, rather than being split geographically.
FY18
2.12
During 2018, the Group issued a series of profit warnings to the London Stock
Exchange (31 July 2018, 24 September 2018, and 27 November 2018). The Group
attributed its poor financial performance to a heatwave in Northern Europe and the
collapse of two major airlines in Germany.
2.13
On 24 September 2018, the Group also announced that its CFO would step down
from the Board on 30 November 2018.

4
IFRS 8 requires the disclosure of information about, inter alia, an entity’s operating segments.
5
Thomas Cook’s German airline

7
2.14
Following the profit warning of 24 September 2018, the Group prepared a revised
business plan and cashflow forecasts for FY19, FY20 and FY21 (the “Revised
Business Plan”). The revisions reduced the forecast EBITDA for each CGU by the
following proportions relative to the original business plan:
CGU
FY19
FY20
FY21
UKTO
-46%
-36%
-28%
NETO
-18%
-10%
-9%
CETO
-24%
-16%
-12%
GAS
-1%
0%
0%
2.15
The Revised Business Plan was approved by the Board on 27 November 2018. The
Group concluded, in light of the Revised Business Plan and its updated FY18 year-
end Goodwill impairment assessment based on it, that Goodwill was not impaired.
2.16
Around this time, and in order to mitigate against a future breach, the Group pursued
a reset of its banking covenants for Q1/Q2 FY19 and Q1/Q2 FY20.
2.17
In late October/early November 2018 a partner in EY’s Restructuring Department
(“the Restructuring Partner”) and a manager in that same team (“the
Restructuring Manager”) (together the “Restructuring Team6”) joined the Audit
Team. Prior to EY tendering for the Group’s FY17 Audit, the Restructuring Partner
had been Global Client Service Partner for the Group, a role that they had held from
2014 until Mr Wilson assumed this role on commencement of the FY17 Audit.7 The
Respondents engaged the Restructuring Team to assist with the audit of Going
Concern. The output of this work, which included an analysis of the forecast covenant
and liquidity headroom with sensitivities and a review of management’s assumptions,
represented a substantial part of the FY18 Audit work performed on Going Concern.
2.18
Between 2 October 2017 and 28 November 2018, the Company’s share price fell by
70% from 121.7p to 36.08p per share.
2.19
Given issues identified with the Group’s forecast covenant compliance, the Audit
Team considered whether a material uncertainty existed which could cast significant

6
Together with a further manager in the Restructuring Department who also assisted with the audit of

Going Concern later in November (see paragraph 5.99 below).
7
The Restructuring Partner had no involvement in the FY17 Audit.

8
doubt on the Group’s ability to continue as a Going Concern. An EY Professional
Standards Panel was convened during the FY18 Audit to consider material
uncertainty, together with other matters.
2.20
The covenant resets referred to at paragraph 2.16 were agreed by the banks in late
November 2018, shortly before the signing date of the FY18 Independent Auditor’s
Report (“FY18 Audit Report”).
2.21
The FY18 Financial Statements were approved for issue on 28 November 2018. The
Group Income Statement reported revenue of £9.584 billion, gross profit of £1.933
billion and a loss after tax for the year of £(163) million. The Group Balance Sheet
reported total assets of £6.569 billion, total liabilities of £6.278 billion, and therefore
net assets of £291 million. Audit materiality was set at £14 million.
2.22
The FY18 Financial Statements accounted for £2.6 billion of Goodwill. This
represented 39% of the Group’s total assets and was still the largest single item on
the balance sheet. Goodwill was not subject to any impairment in the FY18 Financial
Statements.
2.23
The FY18 Audit Report was signed by Mr Wilson on 28 November 2018. It was
unmodified and noted no material uncertainty relating to the use of the Going Concern
assumption.
2.24
As with the FY17 Audit, the Respondents did not consider Goodwill to be a
‘Significant Risk.’ The Respondents initially did not consider Going Concern to be a
‘Significant Risk’ but it was upgraded to a ‘Significant Risk’ in early November 2018.
Goodwill and Going Concern were included as ‘Key Audit Matters’ in the FY18 Audit
Report. They were also included as “significant issues in relation to the financial
statements” that were considered by the Audit Committee in the FY18 Corporate
Governance Report.
2.25
Note 12 to the FY18 Financial Statements included a sensitivity analysis for the
UKTO CGU, which held £1 billion of the £2.6 billion Goodwill balance. It disclosed
that a reasonably possible change in the UKTO CGU future cash flows would result
in the CGU’s carrying amount exceeding the VIU8. The note also stated that the VIU
calculations performed as at 30 September 2018 indicated that the CETO, NETO and

8
This would suggest that the Goodwill balance should be impaired (see paragraph 5.3 below).

9
GAS CGUs were not sensitive to reasonably possible changes in the key
assumptions.
FY 2019
2.26
The Group continued to fall short of its forecasts. On 7 February 2019, Thomas Cook
confirmed that it had commenced a strategic review of its airline business.
2.27
The Group’s interim financial statements for the six months ended 31 March 2019
were issued on 16 May 2019. Performance had still not improved. Sales were lower
than forecast and down relative to the equivalent point in FY18. The Group sustained
an underlying first-half loss on an earnings before interest and tax basis of £245m.
The Group prepared revised forecasts for the full year, taking account of performance
to date. These revised forecasts reduced the expectations for the performance of the
UKTO business and the directors of Thomas Cook decided to fully impair Goodwill in
the UKTO CGU as at 31 March 2019, resulting in Goodwill being written down from
over £1 billion to zero.
2.28
The interim financial statements also included a ‘Material Uncertainty Related to
Going Concern’ paragraph in EY’s Independent Review Report. The revised
forecasts had shown that the Group would require additional liquidity to continue
trading. Although a £300m nine month bridging facility was agreed in principle with
the Group’s banks, it was not executed when the interim financial statements were
issued. The directors recognized that there was uncertainty surrounding the outcome
of the strategic review and this new financing arrangement and concluded that these
matters could cast significant doubt on the ability of the Group to continue as a Going
Concern.
2.29
On 12 July 2019 the Group reported that it was pausing its strategic review and would
not be proceeding with a sale of its airline or tour operator business. It also reported
that it was pursuing a recapitalization plan involving £750 million of new money. The
Group progressed the recapitalization plan during July and August 2019 and agreed
key terms with the relevant parties during this period. Ultimately however, the Group
was unable to secure agreements with key stakeholders. The Group’s directors
subsequently concluded on 22 September 2019 that Thomas Cook was insolvent
and should be placed into compulsory liquidation with immediate effect.
2.30
The liquidation of Thomas Cook resulted in approximately 9,000 redundancies, the
closure of over 500 retail stores and over 1,000 companies and government entities

10
being owed money. Over 140,000 customers had to be repatriated to the UK, at an
estimated cost of £83 million to the taxpayer.

11
3.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
3.1
As noted above, the Statutory Audit Firm and Statutory Auditor responsible for the
FY17 Audit and FY18 Audit were EY and Mr Wilson respectively. In this regard:
(i)
In 2017, EY was ranked as the fourth largest audit firm in the UK, with audit
revenues of £442 million and 116 audit principals. In 2018, EY’s audit
revenues were £458 million and it had 115 audit principals.
(ii)
In 2017, Mr Wilson was a partner of EY, with over 30 years’ statutory audit
experience. His focus in the 15 years prior to the FY18 Audit was on FTSE
100 companies where he acted as the lead audit partner.
(iii) The FY17 Audit was the first audit for which EY and Mr Wilson were,
respectively, the Statutory Audit Firm and Statutory Auditor of the Group.
3.2
The Respondents’ statutory responsibility was to form an opinion as to whether the
FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements showed a true and fair view and had been
properly prepared in accordance with the Companies Act 2006 and Applicable
Accounting Standards (including IAS 1: Presentation of Financial Statements
(“IAS 1”) and when accounting for Goodwill, IAS 36: Impairment of Assets (“IAS
36”)). The Relevant Requirements applicable to the FY17 Audit and FY18 Audit
include the International Standards on Auditing (“ISAs”) and the Ethical Standard
2016.
3.3
As set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice, there were serious failings in the
manner in which the FY17 and FY18 Audits were performed. The breaches of
Relevant Requirements in this Final Settlement Decision Notice relate to
inadequacies in two fundamental areas of audit work (which occurred over two
separate audit years in respect of (i) and (ii) below), and in relation to one overarching
principle (see (iv) below):
(i)
The auditing of the Group’s impairment testing of Goodwill during the FY17
Audit (“Goodwill FY17”).
(ii)
The auditing of the Group’s impairment testing of Goodwill during the FY18
Audit (“Goodwill FY18”).
(iii) The auditing of the Company’s Going Concern Assessment during the
FY18 Audit (“Going Concern FY18”).

12
(iv) The failure to adequately consider a risk to EY’s independence during the
FY18 Audit and the application of safeguards (“Independence FY18”).
3.4
Ultimately, as a result of the Respondents’ breaches of Relevant Requirements, in
the areas of Goodwill (for FY17 and FY18) and Going Concern (for FY18) both of the
FY17 and FY18 Audits failed in their principal objective: that of providing reasonable
assurance that the FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements were free from material
misstatement.
3.5
The applicable Relevant Requirements and the Respondents’ breaches of Relevant
Requirements in relation to the FY17 and FY18 Audits are described in more detail
in sections 4 and 5 of this Final Settlement Decision Notice. However, in summary
the breaches concern:
(i)
A lack of sufficient appropriate audit evidence - An auditor is required
to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence (as defined in ISA 500) to
be able to draw reasonable conclusions about the amounts and
disclosures in the financial statements in order to give reasonable
assurance that the financial statements are free from material
misstatement, whether caused by fraud or error. The Respondents failed
to obtain sufficient evidence to support and adequately corroborate certain
key assumptions and estimates which were included in management’s
assessments of (in FY17 and FY18) Goodwill impairment and (in FY18)
Going Concern.
(ii)
A lack of professional scepticism - An auditor is also required by ISA
200.15 to “plan and perform an audit with professional scepticism
recognizing that circumstances may exist that cause the financial
statements to be materially misstated…the auditor shall maintain
professional scepticism throughout the audit, recognising the possibility of
a material misstatement due to facts or behaviour indicating irregularities,
including fraud, or error, notwithstanding the auditor's past experience of
the honesty and integrity of the entity's management and of those charged
with governance.” Professional scepticism includes consideration of the
sufficiency and appropriateness of audit evidence obtained in the light of
the circumstances. The Respondents accepted without adequate
challenge that there was significant headroom on each of the CGUs and
that because of that headroom, the impairment testing was not particularly

13
sensitive to changes in the assumptions being made by Thomas Cook. In
respect of Going Concern the Respondents failed to challenge
management adequately on their forecasting accuracy, sensitivity testing
and on the level of liquidity headroom.
(iii) Inadequate disclosure in the FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements –
The information presented in the FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements in
relation to Goodwill was not fully reliable and understandable as required
by the applicable financial reporting framework.
(iv) The failure to adequately consider a risk to EY’s independence during
the FY18 Audit – The Restructuring Partner’s long association with the
Group and longstanding and close business relationship with the CFO (as
a result of past work on behalf of EY), amounted to a “Familiarity threat”9
which created a risk to EY’s independence within the meaning of the
Ethical Standard 2016. The Respondents failed to take sufficient steps to
ensure that the Restructuring Partner’s long association with the Group
and senior members of the finance team was properly considered. In so
doing they also failed properly to evaluate whether additional safeguards
were required.
(v)
A failure to prepare sufficient audit documentation - This failure is
evident in all four areas of the Audit summarised at (i) to (iv) above.
3.6
As the Senior Statutory Auditor responsible for the FY17 and FY18 Audits, Mr Wilson
was responsible for the overall quality of the Audits and the direction, supervision,
and performance of the Audits in compliance with the professional standards and
applicable legal and regulatory requirements. Accordingly, Mr Wilson is responsible
for all breaches of Relevant Requirements in relation to the FY17 and FY18 Audits.
3.7
Further as the Statutory Audit Firm responsible for the Audit, EY is responsible for all
breaches of Relevant Requirements on the part of its partners or employees.
3.8
It should be noted that:
(i)
Whilst this Final Settlement Decision Notice identifies and explains failings
in the Respondents’ audit work it does not assert that any balances or
amounts were in fact misstated. However, there was information available

9
As defined under the Ethical Standard 2016.

14
to the Respondents in FY18 which indicated a particularly high risk that the
Goodwill balance for the UKTO may have been impaired. Whilst the audit
work conducted to assess Going Concern was inadequate – in that the
Respondents did not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence in order
to be able to conclude on whether a material uncertainty existed - and
breached Relevant Requirements, it is not alleged that there was in fact a
material uncertainty or that the adoption of the Going Concern basis of
accounting was not appropriate. The conclusions of the Executive Counsel
are based on an analysis of the available evidence; the purpose of her
investigation is not to reperform the Audits.
(ii)
Further, while this Final Settlement Decision Notice explains the
shortcomings in the Respondents’ audit work during the FY18 Audit in
failing to adequately consider a risk to EY’s Independence involving the
Restructuring Partner, it does not assert that there was an actual loss of
Objectivity or lack of Integrity on the part of either the Restructuring Partner
or by the Respondents.
3.9
This Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out the following Sanctions imposed on
the Respondents:
Against EY:
(i)
A financial sanction of £6,500,000, discounted for admissions and early
disposal by 25% so that the financial sanction payable is £4,875,000. The
financial sanction shall be paid no later than 28 days after the date of this
Final Settlement Decision Notice;
(ii)
A published statement in the form of a Severe Reprimand;
(iii) A declaration that the FY17 and FY18 Audit Reports signed on behalf of
EY did not satisfy the Relevant Requirements, as set out in this Final
Settlement Decision Notice; and
(iv) An order to take action to prevent recurrence of the breaches as detailed
at paragraph 6.3.4 below.
Against Mr Wilson:
(i)
A financial sanction of £140,000, discounted for admissions and early
disposal by 25% so that the financial sanction payable is £105,000.

15
(ii)
A published statement in the form of a Severe Reprimand; and
(iii) A declaration that the FY17 and FY18 Audit Reports signed by Mr Wilson
did not satisfy the Relevant Requirements, as set out in this Final
Settlement Decision Notice.

16
4.
RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
4.1
Rule 1 of the AEP states that Relevant Requirements has the meaning set out in
regulation 5(11) of the Statutory Auditors and Third Country Auditors Regulations
2016 (“SATCAR”). The Relevant Requirements include, but are not limited to, the
ISAs issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The
Respondents were obliged to comply with the ISAs when conducting the FY17 and
FY18 Audits. The Relevant Requirements also extend to particular provisions of the
Ethical Standard 2016.
4.2
The ISAs (UK versions) relevant to Executive Counsel’s Final Settlement Decision
Notice are those effective for audits of financial statements for periods ending on or
after June 201610.
4.3
The Relevant Requirements referred to in this Final Settlement Decision Notice are
the following:
(i)
ISA 200 (Overall objectives of the independent auditor and the conduct of
an audit in accordance with international standards on auditing);
(ii)
ISA 220 (Quality Control for an Audit of Financial Statements);
(iii) ISA 230 (Audit Documentation);
(iv) ISA 260 (Communication with Those Charged with Governance);
(v)

Goodwill FY17
Background
5.1
The £2.6 billion of Goodwill included in the Group’s balance sheet arose
predominantly from mergers with MyTravel Group plc, Thomas Cook AG and Co-op
Travel, and from the Company’s acquisition of Condor from Lufthansa.
5.2
Goodwill arises on the acquisition of one business by another. Under IFRS 3, the
acquirer has to assess the value of the assets and liabilities it has acquired. The
identifiable assets and liabilities can include items that may not have been on the
acquiree’s balance sheet, such as the brand name. The residual amount paid by the
acquirer over and above the value of those assets and liabilities is recognised in the
group financial statements as Goodwill. It is an intangible asset that represents: “the
future economic benefits arising from other assets acquired in a business
combination that are not individually identified and separately recognised11.”
5.3
When accounting for Goodwill (post-acquisition), the Group was required to apply
IAS 36. IAS 36 explains (1) assets are to be carried at no more than their recoverable
amount, which is the amount that can be earned from selling or using the asset (i.e.
the value in use or VIU (see paragraph 2.9 above)), and (2) if the carrying value is
greater than the recoverable amount, it is described as “impaired” and an impairment
loss is recognised in the financial statements. For assets such as Goodwill, where
the recoverable amount cannot be determined at the individual asset level (because
Goodwill does not generate cashflows independently of other assets) the recoverable
amount is determined at the level of the CGU12 (which is the smallest group of assets
that generate cashflows independently of other assets).
5.4
Note 12 to the FY17 Financial Statements (Intangible Assets) stated that the Group
assessed Goodwill impairment by comparing the carrying value (“CV”) of each CGU’s
assets and liabilities to the VIU (i.e. cashflows) expected to be generated by the
CGUs in the future.
5.5
The Group’s VIU calculations for the purpose of its impairment testing were based on
assumptions in the FY18-FY21 business plan (the “FY18-FY21 Business Plan”)

C.
Going Concern FY18
Background
5.82
The Going Concern assumption is fundamental to the preparation of financial
statements and a key consideration for any Statutory Auditor to address. The
principal accounting standard that Thomas Cook was required to apply was IAS 1:
Presentation of Financial Statements. IAS 1 requires management to make an
assessment of an entity’s ability to continue as a Going Concern. It also states that
an entity shall prepare its financial statements on a Going Concern basis unless
management intends to liquidate the entity or to cease trading, or has no realistic
alternative but to do so. This requirement applies even when there are uncertainties
about events or conditions that may cast significant doubt upon the entity’s ability to
continue as a Going Concern in the future. Such uncertainties are required to be
disclosed in the financial statements when they are material.
5.83
In considering whether a company/group is a Going Concern, the key test is therefore
whether the company/group can pay its debts as they fall due for a period of not less
than twelve months from the date the financial statements are approved. If the Going
Concern assumption is not appropriate, the company/group prepares its accounts on
a break-up basis, with assets valued on the basis of expected realisation from a
forced sale.
5.84
IAS 1 explains that: (1) when management is aware, in making its Going Concern
assessment, of material uncertainties related to events or conditions that may cast
significant doubt upon the entity's ability to continue as a Going Concern, the entity
shall disclose those uncertainties44; and (2) when an entity has a history of profitable
operations and ready access to financial resources, the entity may reach a conclusion
that the Going Concern basis of accounting is appropriate without detailed analysis.
In other cases, management may need to consider a wide range of factors relating
to current and expected profitability, debt repayment schedules and potential sources
of replacement financing before it can satisfy itself that the Going Concern basis is
appropriate45.
5.85
Sensitivity testing, stress testing and scenario analysis are mechanisms used to
assess the risks facing a business and the potential impacts if those risks were to

44

materialise. The purpose is to analyse the effect of changes to the assumptions
incorporated in a financial model. Strictly sensitivity testing involves changing one
variable at a time, whereas scenario testing involves changing multiple variables,
however the terms are sometimes used interchangeably. For example, in a Going
Concern context, the risk being considered could be a decline in demand for a
company’s products. Sensitivity testing might focus on the sales assumptions about
sales volumes and/or values. Analysis would also consider how the company might
mitigate any negative impacts.

5.112
The Respondents were aware that Thomas Cook’s Going Concern assessment was

5.113
Management’s assessment of Thomas Cook’s ability to continue as a Going Concern
involved making judgements about uncertain future outcomes, viz. the forecast
trading and availability of future cash resources set out above. The potential effects
of inherent limitations on the auditor’s ability to detect material misstatements are
greater for future events or conditions that may cause an entity to cease to continue
as a Going Concern. The auditor cannot predict such future events or conditions. The
necessary audit work is inherently more challenging than other lower risk areas.
Professional scepticism and rigorous challenge of management are especially
important in such audits when evaluating management’s Going Concern
assessment.
5.114
In determining the extent of the risk as to whether a material uncertainty existed in
relation to Thomas Cook’s ability to continue as a Going Concern, the Respondents:
