6.4
Having assessed the nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the breaches, the
Executive Counsel has identified the following combination of Sanctions as
appropriate against Mr Wilson:
6.4.1
A financial sanction of £140,000, discounted for admissions and early
disposal by 25% so that the financial sanction payable is £105,000. The
financial sanction shall be paid no later than 28 days after the date of the
Final Settlement Decision Notice;
6.4.2
A published statement in the form of a Severe Reprimand; and
6.4.3
A declaration that the FY17 and FY18 Audit Reports signed by Mr Wilson
did not satisfy the Relevant Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement
Decision Notice.
6.5
In reaching this decision, the Executive Counsel has considered the following matters
in accordance with the Policy.
Nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the breaches
6.6
The breaches of Relevant Requirements feature serious audit failings in two
important areas of the financial statements: Goodwill (for FY17 and FY18) and Going
Concern (for FY18). As a result, both the FY17 and FY18 Audits failed in their
principal objective: to provide reasonable assurance that the FY17 and FY18
Financial Statements were free from material misstatement.
6.7
The Goodwill balance amounted to £2.6 billion and comprised approximately 40% of
the Group’s total assets for both FY17 and FY18. It was therefore necessary that the
Respondents approached this audit area with sufficient scepticism in order to properly
challenge and corroborate the assumptions and estimates in support of
management’s Goodwill impairment model. Regrettably, that did not happen in either
of the FY17 or FY18 Audits. The failings for the audit of Goodwill in FY18 are
particularly serious given Thomas Cook’s deteriorating trading performance, which
presented the heightened risk that the Goodwill balance for the UKTO CGU may have
been impaired.

86
6.8
Going Concern in FY18 was rightly identified as a significant audit risk, however the
procedures performed by the Respondents in response were inadequate and there
were serious audit failings as a result. The Respondents failed to adequately
challenge management with regards to sensitivity testing and liquidity headroom and,
on the basis of the evidence obtained, they were not in a position to properly conclude
on whether a material uncertainty existed. Given the known issues concerning
Thomas Cook’s forecasting accuracy and liquidity headroom, significant further work
should have been performed by the Respondents, particularly in light of Thomas
Cook’s deteriorating financial performance and the issues identified with its forecast
covenant compliance.
6.9
The Relevant Requirements breached embraced the entire audit process in the areas
of Goodwill impairment and Going Concern and included areas such as risk
assessment, the performance of procedures as to obtaining and evaluating audit
evidence, communication with those charged with governance and disclosures. They
feature breaches of key auditing standards dealing with the exercise of professional
scepticism, partner supervision and audit documentation which are central to the
performance of an audit. The failings also include a failure to adequately consider a
risk to independence. The Relevant Requirements breached were thus extensive and
important.
6.10
It is not asserted that the FY17 or FY18 Financial Statements were in fact misstated,
however as a result of the breaches of Relevant Requirements set out in this Final
Settlement Decision Notice the Respondents failed to obtain reasonable assurance
that the FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements were free from material misstatement.
It is therefore asserted that there was at least the risk that the Financial Statements
were materially misstated.
6.11
Paragraphs 2.26 to 2.30 above summarise the events that occurred following the
FY18 Audit. The Group issued interim financial statements for the six months ended
31 March 2019 on 16 May 2019 in which the Group prepared revised forecasts for
the full year and the directors of Thomas Cook decided to fully impair Goodwill in the
UKTO, resulting in Goodwill of over £1 billion being written off. The financial
statements also included a ‘Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern’
paragraph in EY’s Independent Review Report.
6.12
The Executive Counsel is not in a position to positively assert that the FY18 Financial
Statements would have been presented differently absent the breaches, including

87
whether there would have been an impairment of Goodwill or a Material Uncertainty
relating to Thomas Cook’s Going Concern status (see paragraph 3.8 above). It may
therefore be the case that the information presented to stakeholders when the FY18
Financial Statements were published in December 2018 would have been the same
even if the audit work had been performed in accordance with Relevant
Requirements. However, given the lack of assurance obtained by the Respondents
following their audit work in the key areas of Goodwill impairment and Going Concern,
the breaches had the potential to adversely affect a significant number of
stakeholders in circumstances where, absent the breaches, stakeholders might have
been in possession of information regarding Material Uncertainty and Goodwill
impairment earlier than 16 May 2019 which could have enabled them to take different
decisions in the interim to achieve a more favourable outcome.
6.13
Given the matters set out above, the breaches could harm investor, market and public
confidence in the truth and fairness of published financial statements. Whilst the
Executive Counsel does not allege that the breaches by the Respondents caused the
liquidation of Thomas Cook or the consequential loss of significant sums of money,
the breaches had the potential to significantly undermine confidence in (i) the
standards of conduct in general of Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms, and
(ii) Statutory Audit. Moreover, the Respondents were subject to a significant public
interest duty in carrying out the Audits in compliance with relevant standards: Thomas
Cook was a prominent FTSE 250 listed company, “one of the world’s leading travel
groups” (as it described itself in both the FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements) and
a household name within the UK.
6.14
The core audit failings relating to the impairment of Goodwill, a key audit area, were
repeated over two audit years. The breaches in relation to Going Concern and
Independence relate only to one audit year.
6.15
Certain deficiencies, similar to the breaches of Relevant Requirements in this case,
were identified by the FRC’s AQR team in the course of their 2014, 2015, 2016 and
2017 inspections of other EY audits.
6.16
In 2023, EY was the third largest audit firm in the UK, with total fee income of £3,755
million.
6.17
EY was paid a total of £6 million in audit fees for the Audits. It did not however stand
to gain any profit or benefit from the breaches.

88
6.18
It is not suggested that the breaches were intentional, dishonest, deliberate or
reckless.
6.19
EY has been subject to three previous FRC enforcement outcomes in the last five
years.66
6.20
EY has introduced a number of changes and improvements to their audit processes
since the Audits were performed which reduce the risk of recurrence of the breaches.
However, the Executive Counsel considers the risk of recurrence can be further
reduced by way of the above non-financial sanction.
6.21
Mr Wilson was a very senior audit partner at EY with over 30 years of statutory audit
experience. His focus in the 15 years prior to the FY18 Audit was on FTSE 100
companies where he acted as the lead audit partner.
6.22
Mr Wilson has now retired from EY and is no longer a Statutory Auditor. At the time
of his retirement Mr Wilson had an unblemished compliance and regulatory history
with the FRC and ICAEW.
Aggravating and mitigating factors
6.23
There are no aggravating or mitigating factors that exist that have not already been
taken into account in relation to the nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the
breaches set out above. While EY has been subject to three recent previous
disciplinary outcomes, these do not amount to such poor disciplinary history as to
merit any increase in the Sanctions against the firm. While Mr Wilson was a very
experienced audit partner with over 30 years of experience, balanced with his clean
disciplinary history this is not considered to merit any adjustment in the Sanctions
against him.
Deterrence
6.24
Having considered the matters set out at paragraphs 72 and 73 of the Policy, the
Executive Counsel considers that no adjustment for deterrence is required in this
case.

with integrity and objectivity and to maintain their independence (or to
ensure that others do so); to be able to demonstrate that any conditions
or relationships that exist, taking account of any safeguards
implemented, would not compromise the independence of the firm or any
covered person.
Supporting Ethical
Provision 2.6
All partners and staff of the firm and all other covered persons shall
remain alert to conditions or relationships which could compromise the
independence of the firm or any covered person.
Paragraph 1.73
The engagement partner shall ensure that his or her consideration of the
integrity, objectivity and independence of the firm and covered persons
is appropriately documented on a timely basis.
International Accounting Standards (“IASs”)
IAS 1
Presentation of Financial Statements
Paragraph 25
When preparing financial statements, management shall make an
assessment of an entity’s ability to continue as a going concern. An entity
shall prepare financial statements on a going concern basis unless
management either intends to liquidate the entity or to cease trading, or
has no realistic alternative but to do so. When management is aware, in
making its assessment, of material uncertainties related to events or
conditions that may cast significant doubt upon the entity’s ability to
continue as a going concern, the entity shall disclose those uncertainties.
When an entity does not prepare financial statements on a going concern
basis, it shall disclose that fact, together with the basis on which it
prepared the financial statements and the reason why the entity is not
regarded as a going concern.
Paragraph 26
In assessing whether the going concern assumption is appropriate,
management takes into account all available information about the future,
which is at least, but is not limited to, twelve months from the end of the
reporting period. The degree of consideration depends on the facts in
each case. When an entity has a history of profitable operations and
ready access to financial resources, the entity may reach a conclusion
that the going concern basis of accounting is appropriate without detailed
analysis. In other cases, management may need to consider a wide
range of factors relating to current and expected profitability, debt
repayment schedules and potential sources of replacement financing
before it can satisfy itself that the going concern basis is appropriate.

99
IAS 36
Impairment of Assets
Paragraph 30
The following elements shall be reflected in the calculation of an asset’s
value in use:
a) an estimate of the future cash flows the entity expects to derive
from the asset;
b) expectations about possible variations in the amount or timing of
those future cash flows.
Paragraph 32
The elements identified in paragraph 30(b), (d) and (e) can be reflected
either as adjustments to the future cash flows or as adjustments to the
discount rate. Whichever approach an entity adopts to reflect
expectations about possible variations in the amount or timing of future
cash flows, the result shall be to reflect the expected present value of the
future cash flows, ie the weighted average of all possible outcomes.
Appendix A provides additional guidance on the use of present value
techniques in measuring an asset’s value in use.
Paragraph 33
In measuring value in use an entity shall:
a) base cash flow projections on reasonable and supportable
assumptions that represent management’s best estimate of the
range of economic conditions that will exist over the remaining
useful life of the asset. Greater weight shall be given to external
evidence.

b) base cash flow projections on the most recent financial budgets/
forecasts approved by management, but shall exclude any
estimated future cash inflows or outflows expected to arise from
future restructurings or from improving or enhancing the asset’s
performance. Projections based on these budgets/forecasts shall
cover a maximum period of five years, unless a longer period can
be justified.

c) estimate cash flow projections beyond the period covered by the
most recent budgets/forecasts by extrapolating the projections
based on the budgets/forecasts using a steady or declining
growth rate for subsequent years, unless an increasing rate can
be justified. This growth rate shall not exceed the long-term
average growth rate for the products, industries, or country or
countries in which the entity operates, or for the market in which
the asset is used, unless a higher rate can be justified.
Paragraph 44
Future cash flows shall be estimated for the asset in its current condition.
Estimates of future cash flows shall not include estimated future cash
inflows or outflows that are expected to arise from:
a) a future restructuring to which an entity is not yet committed; or

b) improving or enhancing the asset’s performance.
Paragraph 45
Because future cash flows are estimated for the asset in its current
condition, value in use does not reflect:

100
a) future cash outflows or related cost savings (for example
reductions in staff costs) or benefits that are expected to arise
from a future restructuring to which an entity is not yet committed;
or

b) future cash outflows that will improve or enhance the asset’s
performance or the related cash inflows that are expected to arise
from such outflows.
Paragraph 75
The carrying amount of a cash-generating unit shall be determined on a
basis consistent with the way the recoverable amount of the cash-
generating unit is determined.
Paragraph 81
Goodwill recognised in a business combination is an asset representing
the future economic benefits arising from other assets acquired in a
business combination that are not individually identified and separately
recognised. Goodwill does not generate cash flows independently of
other assets or groups of assets, and often contributes to the cash flows
of multiple cash-generating units. Goodwill sometimes cannot be
allocated on a non-arbitrary basis to individual cash-generating units, but
only to groups of cash-generating units. As a result, the lowest level
within the entity at which the goodwill is monitored for internal
management purposes sometimes comprises a number of cash-
generating units to which the goodwill relates, but to which it cannot be
allocated. References in paragraphs 83–99 and Appendix C to a cash-
generating unit to which goodwill is allocated should be read as
references also to a group of cash-generating units to which goodwill is
allocated.
Paragraph 134
An entity shall disclose the information required by (a)–(f) for each cash-
generating unit (group of units) for which the carrying amount of goodwill
or intangible assets with indefinite useful lives allocated to that unit (group
of units) is significant in comparison with the entity’s total carrying amount
of goodwill or intangible assets with indefinite useful lives:
a) the carrying amount of goodwill allocated to the unit (group of units).

b) the carrying amount of intangible assets with indefinite useful
lives allocated to the unit (group of units).

c) the basis on which the unit’s (group of units’) recoverable amount
has been determined (ie value in use or fair value less costs of
disposal).

d) if the unit’s (group of units’) recoverable amount is based on value
in use:

i.
each key assumption on which management has based its
cash flow projections for the period covered by the most
recent budgets/forecasts. Key assumptions are those to

101
which the unit’s (group of units’) recoverable amount is most
sensitive.

ii.
a description of management’s approach to determining the
value(s) assigned to each key assumption, whether those
value(s) reflect past experience or, if appropriate, are
consistent with external sources of information, and, if not,
how and why they differ from past experience or external
sources of information.

iii.
the period over which management has projected cash flows
based
on
financial
budgets/forecasts
approved
by
management and, when a period greater than five years is
used for a cash-generating unit (group of units), an
explanation of why that longer period is justified.

iv.
the growth rate used to extrapolate cash flow projections
beyond
the
period
covered
by
the
most
recent
budgets/forecasts, and the justification for using any growth
rate that exceeds the long-term average growth rate for the
products, industries, or country or countries in which the entity
operates, or for the market to which the unit (group of units) is
dedicated.

v.
the discount rate(s) applied to the cash flow projections.

e) if the unit’s (group of units’) recoverable amount is based on fair
value less costs of disposal, the valuation technique(s) used to
measure fair value less costs of disposal. An entity is not required
to provide the disclosures required by IFRS 13. If fair value less
costs of disposal is not measured using a quoted price for an
identical unit (group of units), an entity shall disclose the following
information:

i.
each key assumption on which management has based its
determination of fair value less costs of disposal. Key
assumptions are those to which the unit’s (group of units’)
recoverable amount is most sensitive.

ii.
a description of management’s approach to determining the value
(or values) assigned to each key assumption, whether those
values reflect past experience or, if appropriate, are consistent
with external sources of information, and, if not, how and why they
differ from past experience or external sources of information.

(iiA) the level of the fair value hierarchy (see IFRS 13) within
which the fair value measurement is categorised in its entirety

102
(without giving regard to the observability of ‘costs of
disposal’).

(iiB) if there has been a change in valuation technique, the
change and the reason(s) for making it.

f) If fair value less costs of disposal is measured using discounted
cash flow projections, an entity shall disclose the following
information:

i.
the period over which management has projected cash flows.

ii.
the growth rate used to extrapolate cash flow projections.

iii.
the discount rate(s) applied to the cash flow projections.

g) if a reasonably possible change in a key assumption on which
management has based its determination of the unit’s (group of
units’) recoverable amount would cause the unit’s (group of units’)
carrying amount to exceed its recoverable amount:

i.
the amount by which the unit’s (group of units’) recoverable
amount exceeds its carrying amount.

ii.
the value assigned to the key assumption.

iii.
the amount by which the value assigned to the key assumption
must change, after incorporating any consequential effects of that
change on the other variables used to measure recoverable
amount, in order for the unit’s (group of units’) recoverable
amount to be equal to its carrying amount.

title: Sanctions against PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP and Jonathan Hinchliffe
text:
Edited for publication

IN THE MATTER OF
THE EXECUTIVE COUNSEL OF THE FINANCIAL REPORTING COUNCIL
-and-
(1) PRICEWATERHOUSECOOPERS LLP
(2) JONATHAN HINCHLIFFE

FINAL SETTLEMENT DECISION NOTICE
Pursuant to Rule 108 of the Audit Enforcement Procedure

This Final Settlement Decision Notice is a document prepared by Executive
Counsel following an investigation relating to, and admissions made by, the
Respondents. It does not make findings against any persons other than the
Respondents and it would not be fair to treat any part of this document as
constituting or evidencing findings against any other persons since they are not
parties to the proceedings.

1.
INTRODUCTION
1.1. The Financial Reporting Council (the “FRC”) is the competent authority for statutory
audit in the UK and operates the Audit Enforcement Procedure (the “AEP”), revised in
June 2023. The AEP sets out the rules and procedure for the investigation,
prosecution and sanctioning of breaches of Relevant Requirements.
1.2. The AEP contains a number of defined terms and, for convenience, those defined
terms are also used within this document. Where defined terms are used, they appear
in italics.
1.3. This Final Settlement Decision Notice also uses the following definitions:

2

1.3.1.
“FY2019” means the financial year ended 30 April 2019, “FY2019 Financial
Statements” means the consolidated financial statements of Wyelands Bank
plc (the “Bank”) for that period, and “FY2019 Audit” means the statutory
audit of the FY2019 Financial Statements.
1.3.2.
“Respondents” means:
1.3.2.1. PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (“PwC”), which was the Statutory
Audit Firm for the FY2019 Audit.
1.3.2.2. Jonathan Hinchliffe (“Mr Hinchliffe”), who was the Statutory Auditor
for the FY2019 Audit, and signed the FY2019 Audit report on behalf
of PwC on 26 July 2019.
1.4. In accordance with Rule 102 of the AEP, Executive Counsel entered into settlement
discussions with the Respondents.
1.5. A Proposed Settlement Decision Notice was issued by Executive Counsel on 26
September 2024 pursuant to Rule 103 of the AEP in relation to the conduct of the
Respondents in respect of the FY2019 Audit. The Respondents provided written
agreement to the Proposed Settlement Decision Notice, pursuant to Rule 105 of the
AEP, on 4 October 2024. The Convener subsequently appointed an Independent
Reviewer, pursuant to Rule 106 of the AEP, to consider the Proposed Settlement
Decision Notice.
1.6. On 18 October 2024, the Independent Reviewer approved the issuance of this Final
Settlement Decision Notice pursuant to Rule 107(a) of the AEP.
1.7. In accordance with Rule 108 of the AEP this Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out:
1.7.1.
The breaches of Relevant Requirements, with reasons;
1.7.2.
The Sanctions imposed on the Respondents, with reasons; and
1.7.3.
The amount payable in respect of Executive Counsel’s Costs.
1.8. This Final Settlement Decision Notice is divided into the following sections:
1.8.1.
Section 2: Executive Summary of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
1.8.2.
Section 3: Background;
1.8.3.
Section 4: Relevant Requirements to which the breaches relate;
1.8.4.
Section 5: Detail of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
1.8.5.
Section 6: Sanctions; and

3

1.8.6.
Section 7: Costs.
2.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
2.1. As is set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice, there were a number of failures
by the Respondents in the manner in which the FY2019 Audit was conducted. The
breaches of Relevant Requirements relate to six areas of audit work as set out below:
2.1.1.
Audit risk assessment:
2.1.1.1. Failing to: (i) adequately consider audit risks posed by the Bank’s
membership of the Gupta Family Group Alliance (the “GFG
Alliance”), and (ii) identify key developments relevant to the overall
assessment of risk, at the planning stage of the audit;
2.1.1.2. Failing to treat the risk around the completeness of related party
disclosures as elevated;
2.1.1.3. Failing to adequately consider: (i) the complexity of transactions with
members of the GFG Alliance, or (ii) whether they comprised
significant transactions with related parties, in concluding that the
risks identified at the financial statement and assertion levels were
appropriate;
2.1.1.4. Failing to revisit the risk assessment in respect of compliance with
laws and regulations, in light of correspondence from the Prudential
Regulation Authority (the “PRA”) in June and July 2019; and
2.1.1.5. Failing to revisit the risk assessment in respect of completeness of
related party disclosures, in light of a fee letter indicating that
management’s listing was incomplete.
2.1.2.
Audit of the Bank’s compliance with laws and regulations:
2.1.2.1. Failing to obtain all relevant PRA correspondence; and
2.1.2.2. Failing to react appropriately to the PRA correspondence that was
obtained.
2.1.3.
Audit of the Bank’s related parties and related party transactions:
2.1.3.1. Failing to perform sufficient risk assessment procedures to
understand the type and purpose of related party transactions;

4

2.1.3.2. Failing to document an understanding of management’s controls for
identifying, accounting for and disclosing related party transactions;
2.1.3.3. Failing to obtain and document sufficient appropriate audit evidence
about whether related party relationships and transactions had been
appropriately disclosed; and
2.1.3.4. Failing to exercise adequate professional skepticism in relation to the
refusal by management to disclose a quantitative measure of the
proportion of GFG Alliance introduced business.
2.1.4.
Audit of the Bank’s assessment of going concern:
2.1.4.1. Failing to have proper regard to the PRA’s concerns in the context of
going concern; and
2.1.4.2. Failing to properly challenge the assumptions underlying
management’s going concern assessment, and document the audit
judgments made.
2.1.5.
Audit of the Bank’s loans and advances:
2.1.5.1. Failing to carry out sufficient procedures to understand adequately
the Bank’s lending business; and
2.1.5.2. Failing to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to verify the
existence of some of the loans.
2.1.6.
Audit of the Bank’s provision for Expected Credit Loss (“ECL”):
2.1.6.1. Failing to adequately evaluate whether the “debt stacking”
assumption applied by the Bank was reasonable; and
2.1.6.2. Failing to apply sufficient professional skepticism to other aspects of
the Bank’s ECL approach.
2.2. Section 5 of this Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out the detailed breaches of
Relevant Requirements. This Final Settlement Decision Notice does not make a
finding that the FY2019 Financial Statements were misstated, except in relation to the
related party disclosures as described in Section 5 under Breach 3.
2.3. This Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out the following Sanctions imposed on the
Respondents:

5

2.3.1.
Against PwC:
2.3.1.1. A financial sanction of £4,500,000, adjusted for the mitigating factor
of exceptional co-operation by a reduction of 5% and further
discounted for admissions and early disposal by 32.5%, so that the
amount payable is £2,885,625;
2.3.1.2. A published statement in the form of a Severe Reprimand;
2.3.1.3. A Declaration that the FY2019 Audit report did not satisfy Relevant
Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice;
2.3.1.4. An Order requiring PwC to take specified action with the aim of
preventing the recurrence of the breaches.
2.3.2.
Against Mr Hinchliffe:
2.3.2.1. A financial sanction of £55,000, adjusted for the mitigating factor of
exceptional co-operation by a reduction of 10% and further
discounted for admissions and early disposal by 32.5%, so that the
amount payable is £33,412;
2.3.2.2. A published statement in the form of a Severe Reprimand;
2.3.2.3. A Declaration that the FY2019 Audit report did not satisfy Relevant
Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice.
3.
BACKGROUND
The Respondents
3.1. PwC is the largest audit firm in the UK, with total fee income of £4,139m in 2023 (the
latest year for which figures are available). Of this, £965m was derived from audit
work. In 2023 the firm had 995 partners in total, and 339 individuals qualified to act as
Statutory Auditors entitled to sign audit reports on the firm’s behalf.
3.2. Mr Hinchliffe joined PwC in 2002 and qualified as a Statutory Auditor in 2013. At the
time of the FY2019 Audit he was an employee of PwC, with the job title of Director. He
resigned from PwC and left in April 2024.
3.3. PwC was the Bank's Statutory Audit Firm for the financial years FY2015 to FY2019; for
the first two of these financial years the Bank was under different ownership and had a
different name, as described in paragraph 3.4 below. Mr Hinchliffe carried out the
Statutory Audits of the Bank’s financial statements for FY2015 to 2019, signing the
audit reports on behalf of PwC as Statutory Auditor.

6

The Bank
3.4. The Bank was incorporated in 1980 under a different name. In December 2016 it was
acquired (via two intermediate holding companies and a trust) by a new beneficial
owner (the “Shareholder”), and renamed Wyelands Bank plc. The Shareholder was
the owner (with a family member) of the GFG Alliance of global businesses operating
in a number of industries including steel, aluminium and renewable energy.
3.5. As a credit institution, the Bank was a Public Interest Entity (“PIE”) for statutory audit
purposes. The Bank was regulated by the PRA and the Financial Conduct Authority
from December 2016. The PRA designated the Bank as a Category 4 UK bank,
meaning that it was regarded as having very little capacity individually to cause
disruption to the UK financial system if it were to fail, but difficulties across the whole
sector or subsector had the potential to cause disruption.
3.6. By FY2019 the Bank's business was mainly in trade finance, predominantly in the
metals and commodities sectors and largely funded by deposits from retail customers.
It had grown this business very significantly in the two years since its acquisition by the
Shareholder, chiefly through business linked to the GFG Alliance. This was consistent
with the Regulatory Business Plan (“RBP”) that the Bank presented to the PRA in
2016, which stated that, in its early years, the Bank would source and support low risk
lending opportunities introduced by the GFG Alliance. However, the Bank’s 2018
Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (“ICAAP”) stated that, by April 2019,
the Bank aimed to reduce the proportion of GFG Alliance-introduced business to 65%.
Despite this, the Bank's management reported to its Audit Committee in March 2019
that 84% of the Bank's business was still being introduced by the GFG Alliance.
3.7. The Bank’s primary trade finance product was invoice discounting, which accounted
for £181.7m of the Bank’s total £437.7m loans and advances (before provisions). This
involved the Bank buying the debt owed by the buyer to the seller in relation to a sale
of goods or services (in other words, the invoice). The Bank would buy the invoice
from the seller at a discount, paying the seller the discounted sum immediately, and
would then collect the entire debt from the buyer on the invoice due date. The seller
would have the benefit of certain and early payment of the discounted sum, while the
Bank would profit to the extent of the discount (assuming the buyer paid the debt). In
many instances, the seller was a GFG Alliance member.
3.8. Also included in the Bank’s business were the following asset-based lending products
(the “Asset Based Lending Transactions”):

7

3.8.1.
Block finance loans totalling £31.6m, two of which related to blocks of
receivables purchased from two GFG Alliance members for £18m (the “Block
Finance Loans”). These loans operated in a similar way to invoice
discounting, as described in paragraph 3.7 above, but they related to multiple,
rather than individual, invoices. The sellers acted as collection agents for the
Bank.
3.8.2.
Loans totalling £104.9m to 13 special purpose vehicles (“SPVs”) engaged in
the development and operation of hydropower plants in the UK (the
“Hydropower Loans”). These loans were made primarily to refinance existing
indebtedness to other financiers. The SPVs were previously owned by a GFG
Alliance member but ownership was transferred to third parties at loan
issuance. It was intended that a GFG Alliance member would repurchase the
SPVs, and this transaction would include the repayment of the loans.
3.8.3.
Loans to a GFG Alliance member totalling £32.8m, related to invoices for
steel inventory sold to nine SPVs, where the Bank had retained title security
(the “Retained Title Loans”). While the loan was made to the GFG Alliance
member, the amounts due under the invoices were to be collected from the
SPVs.
3.8.4.
Inventory loans totalling £29.2m, two of which related to steel inventory
purchased by two SPVs from a GFG Alliance member for £27.3m (the
“Inventory Loans”). The loans were made to the SPVs and it was intended
that repayment of the loans would occur upon repurchase of the steel
inventory by the GFG Alliance member.
3.8.5.
Bridging loans totalling £39.9m, related to electricity generators purchased by
five SPVs from a GFG Alliance member (the “Bridging Loans”). While the
loans were made to the SPVs, the GFG Alliance member acted as their agent
in relation to the loans.
PRA correspondence prior to the commencement of work on the FY2019 Audit
3.9. The PRA noted in a letter to the Bank dated 8 March 2018 (the “March 2018 PRA
letter”) that, while the Bank had grown its balance sheet significantly over the
preceding 12 months and this demonstrated the viability of its business model, the
sustainability of the business remained unproven and would take longer to establish. It
was noted that the Bank was working actively to originate more of its own business, as

8

distinct from business sourced from GFG Alliance members. Establishing this
independence would be an important factor in the PRA’s assessment of sustainability.
3.10. The March 2018 PRA letter also reported issues with the Bank's monitoring of capital
adequacy, including data quality, reconciliation and reporting issues, which indicated a
cause for concern around governance. The PRA was concerned at signs that the
Board of the Bank was not challenging matters presented to it, and asked it to continue
to ensure the Bank's plans were not unduly influenced by the Shareholder.
3.11. The PRA raised further concerns in a letter to the Bank dated 12 July 2018 (the “July
2018 PRA letter”). While it acknowledged that the Bank was a new bank with
developing underwriting processes and credit risk management framework, the PRA
identified a number of key areas where development was needed to ensure that the
Bank undertook its business prudentially. It noted that the Bank's risk appetites lacked
granularity, its risk framework was not well-defined, and credit policies and procedures
also needed to be more clearly articulated. The PRA also noted that the total amount
of the Bank’s loans that were overdue exceeded 50% of the Bank's capital base at the
time of its review, and advised the Bank to ensure future late payments were identified
and monitored, and that the risk they posed to the Bank and its stability should be
mitigated.
The FY2019 Financial Statements and Audit
3.12. The FY2019 Financial Statements reported that the Bank and its subsidiaries had total
assets of £856.0m (FY2018: £604.5m), including loans and advances to customers of
£433.7m after provisions (FY2018: £299.1m) and cash and cash equivalents of
£232.8m (FY2018: £65.6m). Total liabilities of £734.3m were reported (FY2018:
£512.8m), including customer deposits of £726.6m (FY2018: £506.2m). The Bank and
its subsidiaries reported a pre-tax profit of £469,000 (FY2018: £39,000).
3.13. FY2019 was the first year in which the Bank had to apply the accounting standard
IFRS 9: Financial Instruments, which set out a new approach to calculating an
allowance for ECL. In the FY2019 Financial Statements the Bank recognised a
provision of £3.9m for ECL, representing 0.9% of the total loan balance.
3.14. The FY2019 Financial Statements stated that the Bank considered members of the
GFG Alliance to be related parties, but the only related party transactions reported with
GFG Alliance members were interest income of £1.2m and other income of £2.0m
(FY18: £3.9m and £0, respectively), and other assets of £0.9m and customer deposits
of £0.7m (FY18: £0 and £26.2m, respectively). The Annual Report stated that:

9

“During our first two years, our rapid growth and strong financial performance has
owed much to our ability to source business through introductions from companies
controlled by our shareholder. This business has been undertaken on commercial
terms, frequently in competition with other banks. Our approach is to treat
shareholder-introduced clients in the same way that we would treat any other
customer.”
3.15. The Annual Report also stated that a goal of the Bank had been to do business with a
wider base of clients, and it aimed in future years to broaden its customer base both in
absolute terms and as a proportion of its business. The Annual Report noted that over
the year the Bank had continued to develop new business streams through Trade
Finance, Asset Based Lending and Asset Finance to third parties.
3.16. In June 2019, while the FY2019 Audit was being carried out, the PRA wrote to the
Bank (the “June 2019 PRA Letter”) giving notice that the Bank had been placed on
the PRA’s watchlist due to concerns including the Bank's reliance on GFG Alliance
companies, a potential breach of large exposure rules, the sustainability of its business
model and the nature and quality of its loan book. The PRA described this watchlist as
a list of firms that the PRA was most concerned about from the perspective of its
statutory objectives.
3.17. On 22 July 2019, the PRA issued a notice under section 166 of the Financial Services
and Markets Act 2000 (the “s.166 Requirement Notice”) requiring the Bank to obtain
a skilled person's report (the “s.166 review”). The report was required to review: (i) the
Bank's exposure in relation to the Hydropower Loans against the large exposure rules
in the Capital Requirements Regulation and guidelines on connected clients, and (ii)
the Bank's procedures for determining large exposures and regulatory reporting, and
to provide a view on the effectiveness of those procedures. The PRA was concerned
that the Hydropower Loans exposures were to parties constituting a “group of
connected counterparties” for the purposes of calculating the Bank's large exposure
risk for capital purposes, on the basis that they were connected to each other. The
PRA also made reference to the degree of influence exercised by GFG Alliance
members and their relationship with the counterparties, and the role of the Bank’s
board and senior executives in ensuring that loans complied with connected client and
related party rules.
3.18. On 26 July 2019, Mr Hinchliffe signed the FY2019 Audit report on behalf of PwC. The
Respondents’ statutory responsibility was to form an opinion as to whether the Bank’s
FY2019 Financial Statements showed a true and fair view and had been properly

10

prepared in accordance with the relevant financial reporting framework and the
Companies Act 2006. PwC’s report on those financial statements stated that they had
been properly prepared in accordance with International Financial Reporting
Standards and that PwC’s audit of them had been conducted in accordance with the
applicable auditing standards.
3.19. The fees for the statutory audit and related assurance services, as reported in the
FY2019 Financial Statements, were £206,000.
Events after the signing of the FY2019 Audit report
3.20. In September and October 2019, the PRA imposed requirements on the Bank to
prevent it from transacting with members of the GFG Alliance and entities introduced
by them, and to restrict the Bank's ability to accept deposits from third parties.
3.21. On 29 November 2019, PwC resigned as the Bank’s Statutory Audit Firm, citing
conflict of interest concerns.
3.22. In March 2020 the PRA varied its requirements, effectively stopping the Bank from
entering into new transactions. Also in March 2020, the Bank's Board decided to effect
a solvent wind down.
3.23. The Bank’s FY2020 financial statements (which were audited by a different firm) report
that in the year to 30 April 2020 some business introduced to the Bank by members of
the GFG Alliance was not performing as intended, resulting in a direct exposure to
GFG Alliance members. These financial statements also refer to the impacts of the
Covid-19 pandemic on the Bank and on global supply chains. A number of the Bank’s
counterparties which had originally been introduced by GFG Alliance members failed

Failures in the initial identification and assessment of risks
5.8. The audit team failed to give adequate consideration to the audit risks posed by the
Bank’s membership of the GFG Alliance at the planning stage of the audit:
5.8.1.
The audit team’s focus, with regard to related party transactions, was on the
disclosures required in the financial statements, and they did not adequately
consider the wider risks that related party matters posed for the audit as a

transactions (including those outside the ordinary course of business) is

below). Significant transactions with related parties are also highlighted as a
relevant consideration when identifying significant risks, in paragraph 28(c)

5.8.2.
The audit team was aware of the extent to which the Bank was closely
involved with other members of the GFG Alliance, by reference to the volume
and nature of the Bank’s GFG Alliance-related business and the explicit
acknowledgement in the Agenda for the Audit Planning Meeting that the main
business activities of the Bank were carried out with a view to providing
funding for members of the GFG Alliance.

14

5.8.3.
Given the level of the Bank’s business with other members of the GFG
Alliance, the audit team should have considered sources of risk arising from
this. In particular the audit team ought to have assessed the risk that, since
PwC was not the auditor of the other members of the GFG Alliance, this could

transactions between members under ultimate common control.
5.8.4.
While potentially a source of risk, the Bank’s involvement with the GFG

5.8.5.
PwC procedures required the audit team to consider whether there were

management or owners, or the legality of their actions. If the audit team had
researched press articles on the Bank and the Shareholder, they would have

there was no adverse publicity about the Bank’s owner.
5.8.6.
The wider risks around the Bank’s involvement with the GFG Alliance were
discussed and acknowledged within PwC in the context of the firm’s
subsequent resignation as auditors. They should have been appropriately
recognised and fully considered during the FY2019 Audit.
5.9. Further, the work undertaken by the audit team to update their understanding of the
Bank’s business for the purposes of the FY2019 Audit failed to identify key
developments relevant to the overall assessment of risk:
5.9.1.
The Bank's business was essentially described in the various planning
documents as invoice discounting. This did not acknowledge the diversity and
complexity of the Bank’s activities. The previous year’s 2018 Annual Report
Summary disclosed that the Bank had four separate products (receivable
finance, trade finance, inventory finance and asset finance).

15

5.9.2.
The planning documents also stated that no new contracts had been entered

additional loans made by the Bank.
5.9.3.
The planning documents also assumed that there were no complex customer

complex, warranting particular care to understand them adequately, and the
use of audit team members with the appropriate levels of skill and experience.
When it became apparent that the Bank was undertaking transactions that
were not simple invoice discounting, the relevant contracts should have been
reviewed to properly understand the transactions and related audit risks, and
to plan how they should be addressed. However, this was not done.
5.9.4.
In that regard, paragraph 103 of the relevant Practice Note issued by the FRC
(Practice Note 19: The Audit of Banks and Building Societies in the United
Kingdom) gives as an example of “specialised activities” requiring particular
consideration when obtaining an understanding of the entity, “trade finance,
invoice discounting and factoring (where the documentation can be complex

5.9.5.
A member of the audit team did prepare a document in April 2019 that sought

5.11. In the FY2018 Audit, disclosure of related party transactions by the Bank had been

5.12. In reaching this decision the audit team failed to have sufficient regard to:

Breach 4 – Audit of the Bank’s assessment of going concern
Relevant ISAs
5.47. ISA 570 is concerned with “the auditor’s responsibilities in the audit of financial
statements relating to going concern and the implications for the auditor’s report”
(paragraph 1).
5.48. Paragraph 2 of ISA 570 explains that “Under the going concern basis of accounting,
the financial statements are prepared on the assumption that the entity is a going
concern and will continue its operations for the foreseeable future”.
5.49. A preamble to the UK version of ISA 570 provides additional assistance with
interpreting the term “going concern” in the UK context:
“The financial reporting frameworks applicable in the UK generally require the
adoption of the going concern basis of accounting in financial statements,
except in circumstances where management intends to liquidate the entity or to
cease trading, or has no realistic alternative to liquidation or cessation of
operations. In effect, an entity that does not meet the threshold for that exception
is described as a going concern. This requirement applies even when there are
uncertainties about events or conditions that may cast significant doubt upon the
entity’s ability to continue as a going concern in the future. Such uncertainties
are required to be disclosed in the financial statements when they are material.
The term going concern assumption is the defining assumption about the
condition of an entity for which adoption of the going concern basis of accounting
is appropriate: that the entity is, and will be able to continue as, a going concern.
Accordingly, as used in this ISA (UK):
A. The term “going concern” applies to any entity unless its management intends
to liquidate the entity or to cease trading, or has no realistic alternative to
liquidation or cessation of operations; and
B. The term “ability to continue as a going concern” is equivalent to the term
“ability to continue to adopt the going concern basis of accounting” in the future.”
5.50. Paragraph 10 of ISA 570 concerns the requirement to perform risk assessment
procedures in paragraph 5 of ISA 315, to which reference has already been made in
the context of Breach 1. Paragraph 10 of ISA 570 required the Respondents, when
performing those procedures, to consider whether events or conditions existed that
may cast significant doubt on the Bank’s ability to continue as a going concern.
5.51. Paragraph 11 of ISA 570 required the Respondents to remain alert throughout the audit
for audit evidence of events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the Bank’s

24

ability to continue as a going concern.
5.52. Paragraph 12D-1 of ISA 570 required the Respondents to maintain professional
skepticism (in accordance with paragraph 15 of ISA 200, to which reference is made
elsewhere) throughout the audit and in particular when reviewing future cash flow
relevant to the Bank’s ability to continue as a going concern.
5.53. The following ISAs of general application are also relevant to the Respondents’
auditing of going concern:
5.53.1. Paragraph 6 of ISA 500 required the Respondents to design and perform
audit procedures that were appropriate in the circumstances for the purpose
of obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence.
5.53.2. Paragraph 8 of ISA 230 required the Respondents to prepare audit
documentation that was sufficient to enable an experienced auditor, having no
previous connection with the audit, to understand the nature, timing and
extent of the audit procedures performed, the results of those audit
procedures and the audit evidence obtained, and the significant matters
arising during the audit, the conclusions reached on those matters and the
significant professional judgments made in reaching those conclusions.
5.54. The Respondents breached these requirements in a number of respects as set out
below. However, it is not alleged that the audit team’s ultimate conclusions were

5.55. The audit team did not properly evaluate the matters set out in the PRA

This was a breach of paragraph 10 of ISA 570 and paragraph 8(a) and (b) of ISA 230.
5.56. By failing to assess or document the impact of the PRA’s communications, the audit

Failure to properly challenge the assumptions underlying management’s going concern
assessment, and document the judgments made
5.58. The assessment of the Bank’s ability to continue as a going concern carried out by the
Bank’s management was based in part on assumptions as to the speed with which the

members. These assumptions were optimistic, in light of the progress made by the

The ability of the Bank to reduce its dependence on GFG Alliance-sourced business
was an important matter, in light of the attention given to the issue by the PRA.
5.59. The audit team did not demonstrate sufficient professional skepticism when assessing
the appropriateness of the growth forecasts and assumptions underlying
management’s going concern assessment. They did not document their challenge to
management in this regard. This was a further breach of paragraph 12D-1 of ISA 570
and paragraph 8(a) and (b) of ISA 230.
Impact of these failures on compliance with subsequent requirements of ISA 570
5.60. Having completed their evaluation of management’s assessment of the Bank’s ability
to continue as a going concern, paragraph 18 of ISA 570 required the Respondents to
reach a conclusion as to whether a material uncertainty existed about the Bank’s
ability to continue as a going concern.
5.61. The audit team did not consider whether the PRA correspondence or the Bank’s
growth forecasts and assumptions gave rise to any significant doubt as to the Bank’s
ability to continue as a going concern. The audit team therefore failed to apply
sufficient professional skepticism in respect of these important matters, as set out
above, and this undermined the reliability of their work over management’s conclusion
that there was no material uncertainty about the Bank’s ability to continue as a going
concern.
Breach 5 – Audit of the Bank’s loans and advances
Relevant ISAs
5.62. ISA 505 is concerned with “the auditor’s use of external confirmation procedures to
obtain audit evidence” (paragraph 1).

26

5.63. Paragraph 2 of ISA 505 notes that “depending on the circumstances of the audit, audit
evidence in the form of external confirmations received directly by the auditor from
confirming parties may be more reliable than evidence generated internally by the
entity”.
5.64. Paragraph 7 of ISA 505 required the Respondents to maintain control over external
confirmation requests when using external confirmation procedures, including
determining the information to be confirmed or requested, selecting the appropriate
confirming party, designing the confirmation requests and sending the requests to the
confirming party.
5.65. Paragraph 12 of ISA 505 required the Respondents to perform alternative audit
procedures to obtain relevant and reliable audit evidence, in the case of each non-
response to an external confirmation request.
5.66. Paragraph 16 of ISA 505 required the Respondents to evaluate whether the results of
the external confirmation procedures provided relevant and reliable audit evidence, or
whether further audit evidence was necessary.
5.67. The following ISAs of general application are also relevant to the Respondents’
auditing of loans and advances:
5.67.1. Paragraph 6 of ISA 500 required the Respondents to design and perform
audit procedures that were appropriate in the circumstances for the purpose
of obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence.
5.67.2. Paragraph 9 of ISA 500 required the Respondents to evaluate whether the
information provided by the Bank was sufficiently reliable for their purposes,
including as necessary in the circumstances obtaining audit evidence about
the accuracy and completeness of the information.
5.67.3. Paragraph 15 of ISA 200 required the Respondents to plan and perform the
audit with professional skepticism, recognizing that circumstances may exist
that cause the financial statements to be materially misstated.
5.67.4. Paragraph 15(a) of ISA 220 required Mr Hinchliffe, as the audit engagement
partner, to take responsibility for the direction, supervision and performance of
the audit engagement in compliance with relevant standards and
requirements (including the ISAs).
5.68. The Respondents breached these requirements in a number of respects as set out
below.

27

Failure to carry out sufficient procedures to understand adequately the Bank’s lending
business
5.69. The audit team was expected to obtain an understanding of the Bank’s business
model, including the commercial rationale for its various classes of loan transactions. A
more detailed understanding was required in the case of significant transactions with
related parties, outside the normal course of business.
5.70. However, the audit team did not perform any audit procedures to assess the terms of
the different classes of loan transactions in detail, or otherwise sufficiently understand
the commercial logic of certain transactions. This would have helped them to
understand how the various classes of transactions were expected to operate, and to
identify several inconsistencies with how some of the loans operated in practice.
Failure to perform such procedures was a breach of paragraph 6 of ISA 500.
5.71. In the absence of such procedures, the audit team did not consider whether any of the
loan agreements contained details that would cause the financial statements to be
materially misstated, and therefore did not apply sufficient professional skepticism.
There was insufficient supervision of the audit team on the part of Mr Hinchliffe, in this
area. There were therefore breaches of paragraph 15 of ISA 200 and paragraph 15(a)
of ISA 220.
5.72. The audit team obtained external confirmation of the loan balances for the Bridging
Loans (see paragraph 3.8.5 above) from the company that sold the generators (a GFG
Alliance member), rather than from the SPVs to whom the money had been lent. The
audit team understood that the GFG Alliance member was an agent in respect of these
loans, and therefore considered it an appropriate party to confirm the loan balances.
However, the audit team did not document their understanding of the role of that
company, or consider the fact that it might mean that the Bank was required to
disclose the loans as related party transactions. This was a breach of paragraph 8(a)
and (b) of ISA 230 and paragraph 15 of ISA 200.
Failure to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to verify the existence of some of the
loans
5.73. To verify the Bank’s loan balances, the audit team sampled loans amounting to
approximately half of the £437m loan book. However, of the loans selected for testing,
the audit team failed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to verify the
existence of certain loans accounting for about a quarter of the amount sampled (one
seventh of the value of the loan book). The various issues affecting different classes of

28

loan are explained below. In each case, the relevant balance exceeded the materiality
threshold for the audit, which was £4.4m.
5.74. In the case of invoice discounting loan balances with a total value of £8.2m, the audit
team obtained external confirmation from the seller (generally a GFG Alliance
member), rather than the buyer, with whom the underlying credit risk was deemed to
reside. The audit team did not assess the individual agreements to evaluate whether it
was appropriate to rely on confirmation from the seller. Where the agreement was that
the buyer pays the Bank directly, obtaining confirmation from the seller provided no
evidence of the existence of the receivable, that the buyer accepted their obligations in
relation to the invoice, or that repayment had not already been made by the buyer. The
audit team therefore failed to properly evaluate whether the external confirmations that
they did obtain provided relevant and reliable audit evidence on their own, and hence
they failed to design and perform audit procedures that were appropriate for obtaining
sufficient appropriate audit evidence in the particular circumstances. This was a
breach of paragraph 16 of ISA 505 and paragraph 6 of ISA 500.
5.75. To the extent that the audit team failed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence
to confirm some of the loan balances and failed to ask for explanations from
management for variances, this was also a breach of paragraph 7(b) of ISA 505 and
paragraph 9(a) of ISA 500.
5.76. Where loan balances could not be verified by external confirmation, the audit team
was required to perform alternative procedures. However, these were not performed
properly.
5.77. In respect of loan balances with a total value of £52.1m, the audit team tested the
initial loan disbursements made by the Bank, despite recording that they were verifying
cash receipts. In respect of one of these balances for a Block Finance Loan of £13.6m,
the audit team recorded (it would seem incorrectly) that the loan was a "roll over"
facility, such that cash receipts were not to be expected.
5.78. Testing loan disbursements did not, on its own, provide sufficient appropriate audit
evidence that the loan was validly recorded at the balance sheet date, and had not, for
instance, already been repaid. This was particularly the case with invoice discounting
transactions, where the original disbursement was paid to the seller rather than the
buyer. Examination of specific subsequent cash receipts is given as a particular
example of alternative procedures in paragraph A18 of ISA 505, and was the obvious
approach in circumstances where the loan was due to be repaid before the date of

29

testing (although this was not the case for all of the loans for which alternative
evidence was being sought).
5.79. In relying solely on initial disbursements rather than subsequent cash receipts or other
available evidence, the audit team failed to perform effective alternative procedures
and failed to design and perform audit procedures that were appropriate for obtaining
sufficient appropriate audit evidence. This was a breach of paragraph 12 of ISA 505
and paragraph 6 of ISA 500.
5.80. Given these failings, the audit work to verify the existence of the loan balances was not
carried out with the required level of professional scepticism and the audit procedures
were not adequately directed. There were therefore breaches of paragraph 15 of ISA
200 and paragraph 15(a) of ISA 220.
Breach 6 – Audit of the Bank’s provisions for ECL
Relevant ISAs
5.81. ISA 540 is concerned with “the auditor’s responsibilities relating to accounting
estimates, including fair value accounting estimates, and related disclosures in an
audit of financial statements” (paragraph 1).
5.82. Paragraph 2 of ISA 540 explains that:
“Some financial statement items cannot be measured precisely, but can only be
estimated. For purposes of this ISA (UK), such financial statement items are
referred to as accounting estimates. The nature and reliability of information
available to management to support the making of an accounting estimate varies
widely, which thereby affects the degree of estimation uncertainty associated
with accounting estimates. The degree of estimation uncertainty affects, in turn,
the risks of material misstatement of accounting estimates, including their
susceptibility to unintentional or intentional management bias”.
5.83. Paragraph 13 of ISA 540 required the Respondents, in responding to the assessed
risks of material misstatement, to undertake one or more of a range of specified
actions, taking account of the nature of the relevant accounting estimate. The action
specified in paragraph 13(b)(ii) is to test how management made the accounting
estimate and the date on which it is based, and in doing so to evaluate whether the
assumptions used by management are reasonable in light of the measurement
objectives of the applicable financial reporting framework.

30

5.84. Paragraph 18 of ISA 540 required the Respondents to evaluate, based on the audit
evidence, whether the accounting estimates in the FY2019 financial statements were
reasonable in the context of the applicable financial reporting framework, or were
misstated.
5.85. Paragraph 15 of ISA 200, requiring the Respondents to plan and perform the audit with
professional skepticism, recognizing that circumstances may exist that cause the
financial statements to be materially misstated, is also relevant to the Respondents’
auditing of ECL.
5.86. The Respondents breached these requirements in a number of respects as set out
below.
Failure to adequately evaluate whether the “debt stacking” assumption applied by the Bank
was reasonable
5.87. It has been noted that the Bank recognised a £3.9m provision for ECL in the FY2019
Financial Statements. Management calculated this amount by the multiplication of
three factors, for each of the Bank’s loans:
5.87.1. Probability of default (“PD”) – the probability of the counterparty going into
default within the relevant period (which could be 12 months or the lifetime of
the loan, depending on whether there had been a significant increase in credit
risk since the loan was made).
5.87.2. Loss given default (“LGD”) – a measure of the loss over the total exposure if
the counterparty went into default.
5.87.3. Exposure at default – the loan balance outstanding at the point of the
borrower going into default, which was taken to be the balance as at the
reporting date.
5.88. The Bank’s approach to determining the PD and LGD for each counterparty used
models that were based on a combination of counterparty or deal specific data,
simplifying portfolio level assumptions, external data and expert judgment. For LGD,
the Bank started with a loss rate of 50% based on observable industry data, but
adjusted it downwards in the case of a number of its exposures, on the assumption
that trade receivables would rank higher than other forms of liability in the event of
default, and so would take a smaller share of the 50% loss. The rationale was that, in
the event of a loan repayment being in default, the obligor would prioritise the payment
of trade creditors in order to mitigate the risk of creditors putting the obligor into an

31

insolvency process. This “debt stacking” assumption had a significant effect on the
LGD element of the calculation, and therefore may have had a significant impact on
the ultimate ECL, although the low PDs across the portfolio limited the potential
impact.
5.89. The audit team did not appropriately evaluate and challenge this important
assumption. This was a breach of paragraphs 13(b)(ii) and 18 of ISA 540.
Failure to apply sufficient professional skepticism to other aspects of the Bank’s ECL
approach
5.90. Given the volume of business introduced by GFG Alliance members and the nature of
the Bank’s loan transactions, the audit team ought to have been more skeptical in
relation to aspects of the Bank’s approach to the calculation of ECL. The audit team
were aware of the inherent limitations of the ECL model and performed audit
procedures to conclude the ECL provision was not materially misstated. However, they
ought to have further challenged whether the specific valuation risks presented by the
structure of the loans introduced by GFG Alliance members were adequately captured
by:
5.90.1. The modelled approach to impairment adopted;
5.90.2. The use and relevance in the ECL calculations of insurance and security (the
latter being a key feature of some loan types); and
5.90.3. The lack of obligor-specific information on which to base the calculations for
multiple loan types (when the Bank should have obtained this information
under its policies and procedures on loan issuance).
5.91. The failure to properly scrutinise these matters, taken together, amounts to a failure to
apply sufficient professional skepticism in respect of the Bank’s approach to ECL, and
therefore a breach of paragraph 15 of ISA 200.
6.
SANCTIONS
6.1
Paragraph 10 of the FRC’s Sanctions Policy (Audit Enforcement Procedure) (the
“Sanctions Policy”) provides that Sanctions are intended to be effective, proportionate
and dissuasive. The reasons for imposing Sanctions are identified in paragraph 11 of
the Sanctions Policy as the following:
6.1.1. to declare and uphold proper standards of conduct amongst Statutory Auditors

32

and Statutory Audit Firms and to maintain and enhance the quality and reliability
of future audits;
6.1.2. to maintain and promote public and market confidence in Statutory Auditors
and Statutory Audit Firms and the quality of their audits and in the regulation of
the accountancy profession;
6.1.3. to protect the public from Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms whose
conduct has fallen short of the Relevant Requirements; and
6.1.4. to deter Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms from breaching the
Relevant Requirements relating to Statutory Audit.
6.2. In considering the Sanctions to be imposed in this case, Executive Counsel has, in
summary, considered the following matters in accordance with the Sanctions Policy.
Nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the breaches
6.3. The breaches of Relevant Requirements were serious and numerous. They affected a
number of different areas of the audit, although they largely stemmed from a single issue:
the failure of the audit team to properly understand the Bank’s lending and therefore the
true extent of its actual and potential exposure to GFG Alliance members. This was
compounded by the failure to appreciate and act on the escalating level of concern
expressed by the PRA about the Bank’s sustainability. The Bank's relationship with the
GFG Alliance and the terms of its lending were central to its business model, and the
failure to properly enquire into and understand those matters was very significant, in the
context of the audit.
6.4. There were a number of breaches of the Relevant Requirements in relation to
professional skepticism and obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence, which are
fundamental to the role of the independent auditor. Some of those breaches were
unrelated to the fundamental issue in relation to the audit team’s understanding of the
Bank’s business mentioned above: for example, the failure to identify the gaps in the
regulatory correspondence, to test management’s related party listing and disclosures
or to verify the existence of particular loan balances.
6.5. As a result of the breaches, the FY2019 Audit failed in its principal objective, namely to
obtain reasonable assurance about whether the FY2019 Financial Statements as a
whole were free from material misstatement. In fact, the related party disclosures note
in the FY2019 Financial Statements was materially restated in FY2020 by the addition
of £21m in outstanding loans and £7m in income, in relation to GFG Alliance members.

33

6.6. The breaches had the potential to adversely affect a significant number of people in
the United Kingdom. As at the FY2019 year-end, the Bank held £727m in customer
deposits from over 15,000 UK public savers. Of this amount, any loss to depositors up
to £657m was protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, and would
ultimately be borne collectively by the financial services industry, which funds that
scheme. The Bank held £233m in cash, but this was only sufficient to cover
approximately a third of the deposits (a further £113m was held as other types of liquid
assets, and £434m of loans and advances).
6.7. The extent to which the sustainability of the Bank was impacted by its exposure to the
GFG Alliance, and the recoverability of loans made to GFG Alliance members, were
highly relevant to the safety of sums deposited with the Bank. Breaches in the auditing
of those matters therefore had the potential to adversely impact the depositors. In the
event, the risk of loss was averted by the intervention of the PRA and by the financial
support provided by the Shareholder in the solvent wind down of the Bank.
6.8. For those reasons, and because the Bank is a credit institution and PIE, the breaches
also had the potential to harm public confidence in the truth and fairness of financial
statements in general, and in the standards of conduct of Statutory Auditors or
Statutory Audit Firms.
6.9. Conversely:
6.9.1. The breaches were limited to one audit year;
6.9.2. They were not intentional or deliberate, reckless or dishonest;
6.9.3. They did not involve financial gain; and
6.9.4. PwC voluntarily carried out a Root Cause Analysis (“RCA”) which identified a
number of changes and improvements already implemented since the FY2019
Audit, which should reduce the likelihood of any recurrence of the breaches.
6.10. The circumstances of the Respondents are also relevant to the determination of
Sanction. PwC is (and was at the time of the FY2019 Audit) the largest audit firm in the
UK. PwC has had Sanctions imposed on it under the AEP on six previous occasions in
the last five years, and in several of those cases the breaches bore some similarity to
those in the present case (although the findings were not available to the Respondents
at the time of the FY2019 Audit).
6.11. Mr Hinchliffe has a clean disciplinary record. As an employee and Director of the firm,
his remuneration was lower than that of partners in large audit firms, who are the

34

individuals most commonly subject to Sanctions under the AEP. Although PwC has
undertaken to pay any financial sanction imposed on him, his lower level of
remuneration is still relevant in determining a proportionate figure for the sanction. This
investigation has had a significant impact on Mr Hinchliffe and was a key factor in his
decision to cease being a Statutory Auditor and to resign from PwC.
6.12. Both Respondents have accepted their responsibility for the breaches and expressed
contrition.
Identification of Sanction
6.13. Having assessed the nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the breaches with
regard to the matters mentioned above, Executive Counsel identified the following
combination of Sanctions as appropriate:
6.13.1. Financial sanctions of £4,500,000 in the case of PwC, and £55,000 in the
case of Mr Hinchliffe.
6.13.2. A published statement in the form of a Severe Reprimand, in the case of each
of them.
6.13.3. A declaration that the FY2019 Audit report did not satisfy the Relevant
Requirements, in the case of each of them.
6.13.4. In the case of PwC, an order requiring the firm to take the following action
which is designed to prevent the recurrence of the contravention:
6.13.4.1.
By 9 July 2025:
(a)
carry out an assessment of the effectiveness of additional
improvement measures identified in or as a result of the
RCA in addressing the specific shortcomings in that audit
(the relevant additional improvement measures and the
manner of the assessment having been agreed by the
FRC in advance); and
(b)
provide a report (the “Report”) which: (i) sets out the
results of the assessment, and (ii) either identifies any
further measures that PwC intends to take to address the
shortcomings, or explains why no such further measures
are necessary.

35

6.13.4.2.
Provide any further information or report, in connection with or
as a result of the Report, as required by the FRC.
Aggravating and mitigating factors
6.14. Executive Counsel has then taken into account any aggravating and mitigating factors
that exist, to the extent that they have not already been taken into account in relation
to the nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the breaches.
Aggravating factors
6.15. There are no aggravating factors that have not already been considered.
Mitigating factors
6.16. All relevant mitigating factors have already been considered, except the level of co-
operation provided by the Respondents. Paragraph 69 of the Sanctions Policy explains
that, since Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms are required to co-operate with
any investigation under the AEP, only an exceptional level of co-operation will be
regarded as a mitigating factor at the point of determining Sanctions.
6.17. During the course of the investigation PwC carried out their own review of the auditing
of ECL, and the RCA in respect of the audit as a whole, and shared the results with
Executive Counsel. Having regard to the timing and impact of these steps, Executive
Counsel considers that they amount to an exceptional level of co-operation worthy of a
discount of 5% to the financial sanction. The financial sanction is therefore reduced to
£4,275,000
6.18. With regard to Mr Hinchliffe, he has shown great professionalism and resilience in
continuing to engage with the investigation in a diligent fashion. Executive Counsel
considers that, in the particular circumstances of this case, this amounts to exceptional
co-operation on his part and that a discount of 10% to the financial sanction against
him is appropriate. The financial sanction is therefore reduced to £49,500.
Deterrence
6.19. Having considered the matters set out at paragraphs 72 and 73 of the Policy,
Executive Counsel considers that no adjustment for deterrence is required in this case.
Discount for Admissions and Settlement
6.20. Having taken into account the full admissions by the Respondents and the stage at
which those admissions were made (at an early point within Stage 1 of the case, in
accordance with paragraph 84 of the Sanctions Policy), Executive Counsel determined

36

that a further reduction in the financial sanctions of 32.5% is appropriate. The financial
sanction against PwC is therefore further reduced to £2,885,625, and the financial
sanction against Mr Hinchliffe is further reduced to £33,412.
